choices: Call background() at the start of draw() to clear the canvas each frame
Draw fewer circles
Use a faster computer
Call noLoop()
evidence: sketch.js
scenarios.hint: What happens to last frame's pixels if nothing erases them — bug or feature?
scenarios.prompt: The artist wants a single clean circle following the mouse, but gets a smeared trail. Fix?
scenarios.situation: A sketch draws an ellipse at the mouse position every frame — but old ellipses never disappear.
scenarios.title: The smearing circle
scenarios.why: Without background() at the top of draw(), each frame paints over the last — the 'trail' effect. Calling background() clears the canvas every frame for clean animation. (Trails are also a beloved technique — achieved deliberately with a translucent background fill — but here they're the bug.)

choices: rect() is broken in this version
The canvas is too small
rect() draws from the corner by default (rectMode(CORNER)), and y grows downward — the rectangle extends right and down from (100, 100)
You must call stroke() first
evidence: sketch.js
rect(100, 100, 60, 40);  // expected: centered at 100,100
scenarios.hint: What do the four numbers to rect() mean by default — and which corner do they start from?
scenarios.prompt: Why isn't the rectangle centered at (100, 100)?
scenarios.situation: An artist expects rect(100, 100, 60, 40) to center a rectangle at (100, 100), but it appears offset down and right.
scenarios.title: The off-center rectangle
scenarios.why: Default rectMode(CORNER): the first two args are the top-left corner, and with y growing downward the rect extends right and down from (100, 100). For centering, call rectMode(CENTER) once in setup(). The coordinate system (origin top-left, y down) is the source of half of all beginner layout bugs.

choices: p5.js has a style cache bug
Every fill() after the red one needs push()/pop() around the red shape to contain the style change
You can't use more than one fill per frame
Call background() between shapes
evidence: sketch.js
scenarios.hint: Drawing state (fill, stroke) persists until changed — how do you sandbox a temporary change?
scenarios.prompt: The third shape renders blue instead of gray. What's wrong?
scenarios.situation: After drawing a red ellipse and a blue rect, a third shape meant to be gray renders blue.
scenarios.title: The leaking fill
scenarios.why: fill() sets persistent drawing state — everything after fill(0,0,255) stays blue until changed. Wrap the blue rect in push()/pop() to sandbox its style, or set fill() again before the third shape. push()/pop() save and restore both styles and transformations; forgetting pop() is the classic state-leak.

choices: fill(180, 80, 90): hue 180 (cyan), saturation 80%, brightness 90%
fill(180, 80, 90): red 180, green 80, blue 90
HSB mode doesn't change fill()
The values are out of range and will error
evidence: sketch.js
scenarios.hint: colorMode(HSB, 360, 100, 100) redefines what the three numbers mean — what does 180 mean on a 360-degree wheel?
scenarios.prompt: What color does fill(180, 80, 90) produce?
scenarios.situation: After colorMode(HSB, 360, 100, 100), an artist writes fill(180, 80, 90).
scenarios.title: The HSB fill
scenarios.why: Hue 180° on the color wheel is cyan, at 80% saturation and 90% brightness. HSB separates 'which color' (hue) from 'how intense' (saturation) and 'how bright' — which is why generative artists love it: sweep the hue for rainbows, fix saturation/brightness for harmony. Forgetting colorMode is active is a classic source of 'wrong color' bugs.

choices: Draw everything twice
Use createGraphics() for an offscreen buffer: compose the static layer once, then image() it each frame
Take a screenshot and load it
It's impossible; everything must redraw
evidence: sketch.js
// 2000 static stars + 50 moving ships; stars redrawn every frame: 12 fps
scenarios.hint: If the stars never change, why pay to redraw them 60 times a second?
scenarios.prompt: How do you hit 60 fps?
scenarios.situation: 2000 static stars plus 50 moving ships: redrawing everything each frame runs at 12 fps.
scenarios.title: The static starfield
scenarios.why: Render the static stars once into an offscreen buffer (let pg = createGraphics(w, h)), then image(pg, 0, 0) each frame and draw only the 50 ships dynamically. Layering static content into buffers is the fundamental performance pattern in creative coding — separate what changes from what doesn't.

choices: The canvas can't change size after setup
Implement windowResized() { resizeCanvas(windowWidth, windowHeight); } and make layout relative
Reload the page on resize
Use fixed pixel positions everywhere
evidence: sketch.js

function setup() { createCanvas(windowWidth, windowHeight); }
// layout uses absolute pixels; breaks on resize
scenarios.hint: p5.js has an event for exactly this — what should it do besides resizing?
scenarios.prompt: How do you make the sketch survive window resizes?
scenarios.situation: A fullscreen sketch breaks its layout when the browser window resizes.
scenarios.title: The resize handler
scenarios.why: Define windowResized() to call resizeCanvas(windowWidth, windowHeight) and recompute any layout cached from the old size. Robust sketches derive positions from width/height (fractions, not absolute pixels) so any canvas size works. Absolute-pixel layouts are the reason 'it worked on my monitor' is a meme.

scenarios.title: Trails Without the Mess
scenarios.situation: You are building a generative piece where particles leave fading trails. Your first attempt redraws the entire scene each frame, so old positions vanish instantly. Your second attempt skips the clear entirely, so the screen eventually becomes a solid blob of overlapping strokes.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct rendering technique to get smooth, gradually fading trails?
choices: Fill the canvas with a low-alpha rectangle each frame instead of clearing it, so previous frames decay gradually
Store every particle position ever drawn and redraw them all each frame with decreasing opacity
Clear the canvas every other frame so trails persist for exactly two frames
Render each particle on a separate offscreen canvas and composite them with blend modes
scenarios.why: Painting a semi-transparent rectangle (e.g., fillStyle rgba(0,0,0,0.05)) over the canvas each frame multiplies the existing pixels toward the background color, creating a natural exponential fade. Redrawing all history is O(n) and blows up memory; skipping clears saturates the image.
scenarios.hint: Think about what happens to pixel values when you paint a translucent color over them repeatedly.
objectives: Apply the translucent-fill technique for motion trails
evidence: Explain why full redraw and no-clear both fail for trails

scenarios.title: Retina-Ready Canvas
scenarios.situation: Your canvas piece looks crisp on your desktop monitor but blurry on a phone and on the client's Retina laptop. You set the canvas width and height attributes to 800x600 and sized it with CSS to 800x600, so you expected identical output everywhere.
scenarios.prompt: How should you fix the blurriness on high-density displays?
choices: Multiply the canvas's pixel dimensions by devicePixelRatio and scale the drawing context by the same factor, keeping CSS size at 800x600
Draw at larger coordinates and let CSS scale the canvas down to 800x600
Replace the canvas with SVG, which is resolution-independent by default
Set image-rendering: crisp-edges in CSS to force sharp rendering
scenarios.why: A canvas has a backing-store size (attributes) separate from its display size (CSS). On a 2x display, 800 backing pixels stretch across 1600 device pixels, blurring. Setting backing size to 800*dpr and ctx.scale(dpr, dpr) keeps your coordinate system at 800x600 while using every physical pixel.
scenarios.hint: The canvas backing store and its CSS box are two different sizes — which one does the GPU rasterize into?
objectives: Handle devicePixelRatio for crisp canvas rendering
evidence: Describe the relationship between canvas attributes, CSS size, and device pixels

choices: Increment x by a fixed amount each frame; frameCount gives you a free clock
Use random() for x each frame
Move x only when the mouse moves
x can't animate without a library
evidence: sketch.js
scenarios.hint: draw() already runs on a clock — what variable counts the ticks?
scenarios.prompt: How do you glide the circle across the screen?
scenarios.situation: A circle should glide smoothly left to right, looping forever.
scenarios.title: The gliding circle
scenarios.why: x = (frameCount * 2) % width: frameCount is a free frame clock, and modulo wraps it. Fixed per-frame increments are the simplest motion; the modulo makes it loop. (For frame-rate independence you'd use deltaTime — but for a first sketch, frameCount is the idiom.)

choices: random() each frame: jumpy and discontinuous
noise(): smooth Perlin noise that wanders organically; advance the noise offset slowly
sin() with a huge frequency
Hardcode positions
evidence: sketch.js
// want: a firefly that drifts organically
scenarios.hint: What's the difference between white noise and Perlin noise over time?
scenarios.prompt: Which function gives the firefly organic drift?
scenarios.situation: A firefly should wander smoothly, not teleport or march in a perfect sine wave.
scenarios.title: The firefly drift
scenarios.why: noise(t) returns smooth Perlin noise — nearby inputs give nearby outputs, so advancing t slowly yields wandering, organic paths. random() jumps discontinuously every call; sin() is too regular. noise() with slowly-advancing offsets (optionally separate offsets per axis) is the signature move of generative motion.

choices: Set x directly to the target; snapping is fine
Move x by a fixed 5 pixels per frame toward the target
x = lerp(x, targetX, 0.05): exponential easing that slows as it approaches
Use random() to jitter toward the target
evidence: sketch.js
// camera should glide toward the mouse, slowing as it arrives
scenarios.hint: What happens to the remaining distance each frame if you always cover 5% of it?
scenarios.prompt: How do you ease the camera toward the mouse?
scenarios.situation: A camera should glide toward the mouse position, decelerating as it arrives.
scenarios.title: The easing camera
scenarios.why: lerp(x, target, 0.05) moves 5% of the remaining distance per frame — fast at first, then asymptotically settling. This exponential ease-out is the most-used motion feel in creative coding (and UI animation). Fixed steps overshoot or crawl; lerp gives the buttery deceleration for free.

choices: Reverse velocity when the ball crosses an edge: if (x > width - r || x < r) vx *= -1
Teleport the ball to the center on hit
Stop the ball at the edge
Delete and respawn the ball
evidence: sketch.js

let x, y, vx, vy;
// ball should bounce around the canvas forever
scenarios.hint: A bounce is a reflection — what happens to the velocity component perpendicular to the wall?
scenarios.prompt: How do you make the ball bounce off the walls?
scenarios.situation: A ball with velocity (vx, vy) should bounce around the canvas forever.
scenarios.title: The bouncing ball
scenarios.why: When the ball's edge crosses a wall, flip the perpendicular velocity component (vx *= -1 for side walls). Account for the radius (x > width - r) so it bounces visually at the edge, not past it. Velocity + boundary reflection is the seed of every physics sketch — gravity, friction, and springs all layer onto this pattern.

choices: if (frameCount == 600) x = 0;
x = (x + speed) % width — modulo wraps the position
Manually detect the edge with a long if-chain
Restart the sketch with location.reload()
evidence: sketch.js
// particle stream should flow right and wrap around seamlessly
scenarios.hint: What arithmetic operation maps any growing number back into [0, width)?
scenarios.prompt: How do you loop the stream seamlessly?
scenarios.situation: Particles flow rightward and should wrap around the left edge seamlessly.
scenarios.title: The seamless wrap
scenarios.why: x = (x + speed) % width wraps any position back into [0, width) — the particle exits right and re-enters left with no pop. Modulo is the looping primitive: it also drives walk cycles, phase wrapping, and tiling. (For perfect GIF loops, make sure the motion period divides the frame count.)

choices: Fixed increments are fine; all screens are 60 fps
Count frames and assume 60 per second
Scale motion by deltaTime (milliseconds since last frame) so speed is real-time regardless of frame rate
Cap the frame rate with frameRate(30) and hope
evidence: sketch.js
x += 3;  // 60fps laptop: smooth. 120Hz display: double speed. Old phone: half speed.
scenarios.hint: If a frame takes twice as long, the object should travel twice as far that frame — what do you multiply by?
scenarios.prompt: How do you keep motion speed consistent across displays?
scenarios.situation: x += 3 per frame runs double-speed on 120Hz displays and half-speed on struggling phones.
scenarios.title: The frame-rate trap
scenarios.why: Multiply by deltaTime (ms since last frame): x += speed * (deltaTime / 1000) moves in real seconds, not frames. Frame-counted motion ties your artwork's timing to the viewer's hardware — deltaTime decouples them. This is the difference between a sketch and a robust piece.

scenarios.title: Frame-Rate Dependent Motion
scenarios.situation: Your animation moves a shape 5 pixels per frame. On your 60fps laptop it glides smoothly, but on a 120Hz display it moves twice as fast, and on a throttled background tab it crawls. A collaborator reports the timing of a 10-second sequence is unpredictable.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct fix so the motion is identical on every display?
choices: Cap the frame rate at 30fps with setInterval so every machine draws the same number of frames
Detect the display refresh rate and adjust the pixel-per-frame value accordingly
Multiply movement by delta time (seconds since the last frame), expressing speed in pixels per second instead of per frame
Use CSS animations instead of requestAnimationFrame for timing guarantees
scenarios.why: Delta-time integration decouples simulation from render rate: position += speed * dt. Frame count varies with display and load, but elapsed seconds are the same everywhere, so a 10-second sequence takes 10 seconds on 30Hz, 60Hz, and 120Hz displays alike.
scenarios.hint: Frames are a variable unit; what unit of time is constant across displays?
objectives: Implement delta-time animation for frame-rate independence
evidence: Convert a per-frame movement to a per-second movement

scenarios.title: Choosing the Right Easing
scenarios.situation: You are animating UI-style cards for an installation's touch screen. The cards should feel physical — settling into place with a slight overshoot, like a spring. You applied a linear tween and it feels robotic; then ease-in-out, which feels floaty but never 'lands'.
scenarios.prompt: Which easing choice gives a convincing spring-like settle, and how should it be implemented?
choices: A longer ease-in-out with more frames, since spring feel is just a matter of duration
A bounce easing curve, which is mathematically identical to a damped spring
An ease-out-back (overshoot) curve for the final segment, or better, a real spring simulation with stiffness and damping so overshoot responds to distance
Linear motion with a fast frame rate, since overshoot is a rendering artifact
scenarios.why: Back easing (overshoot) mimics a spring's settle for fixed tweens, but a true spring integration (velocity += (target-pos)*stiffness; velocity *= damping) handles variable distances and interruptions naturally — the feel stays physical when targets change mid-animation, which easings cannot do.
scenarios.hint: Easing curves map fixed progress to position; what happens when the destination changes halfway through the tween?
objectives: Choose between easing curves and spring physics for motion feel
evidence: Name the situation where a spring simulation beats a fixed easing curve

choices: Nothing can be reproduced; that's the beauty of it
Set randomSeed() / noiseSeed() before generating; same seed replays the piece exactly
Screenshot every run
Avoid random() entirely
evidence: sketch.js
// collector wants to re-mint the exact piece they saw
scenarios.hint: Pseudorandom generators are deterministic — what single value determines the whole sequence?
scenarios.prompt: A collector wants the exact piece they saw re-generated. How?
scenarios.situation: A generative piece uses random() heavily; a collector wants to re-mint the precise variation they previewed.
scenarios.title: The seed as edition
scenarios.why: randomSeed(s) makes the pseudorandom sequence deterministic — same seed, same artwork, every time. The seed becomes the edition number: share it and anyone can re-render the identical piece. This is how generative art platforms (Art Blocks-style) work: the token's seed IS the artwork's DNA.

choices: Perfectly uniform grid; regularity is elegance
Nested loops with noise()-driven variation in size, rotation, and color — controlled irregularity
Place everything with random() and hope
One giant shape in the center
evidence: sketch.js
// 20x20 grid of squares looks dead and mechanical
scenarios.hint: Nature is neither uniform nor chaotic — what sits between a grid and confetti?
scenarios.prompt: How do you make the grid feel alive?
scenarios.situation: A 20×20 grid of identical squares looks dead.
scenarios.title: The living grid
scenarios.why: Drive per-cell parameters with noise(): size = base + noise(x*0.1, y*0.1) * range, slight rotations, hue shifts. Smooth noise gives coherent variation — neighbors relate, nothing repeats mechanically, nothing dissolves into chaos. The grid-plus-noise pattern is the workhorse of generative composition: order as a scaffold, noise as the life.

choices: Copy-paste the branch code 8 levels deep
A recursive function: drawBranch(len) draws a segment, then calls itself twice at smaller lengths and rotated angles
Draw one branch and mirror it with scale(-1, 1)
Recursion can't draw trees
evidence: sketch.js
// want: a branching tree, 8 levels deep
scenarios.hint: A branch looks like a small tree — how do you express 'a tree is branches that end in smaller trees'?
scenarios.prompt: How do you draw the tree?
scenarios.situation: You want a branching tree, 8 levels deep, with natural-looking irregularity.
scenarios.title: The recursive tree
scenarios.why: function branch(len) { line(0,0,0,-len); translate(0,-len); rotate(a); branch(len*0.67); rotate(-2a); branch(len*0.67); } with a base case at small len. Recursion expresses self-similarity directly: each branch is a smaller tree. Add noise() to angles and length ratios for organic feel. Base case required — infinite recursion is a stack overflow, not a tree.

choices: Give each particle position + velocity, update with simple rules (attraction, repulsion, damping), and let the swarm emerge
Hand-animate 500 particles
One particle is enough; systems don't scale
Hardcode every trajectory
evidence: sketch.js
// want: 500 particles that swirl like a murmuration
scenarios.hint: Nobody choreographs a flock — what three local rules produce flocking?
scenarios.prompt: How do you get 500 particles to move like a murmuration?
scenarios.situation: You want a swirling, flocking particle system — not 500 hand-animated dots.
scenarios.title: The murmuration
scenarios.why: Particles with position + velocity following local rules (cohere toward neighbors, separate when crowded, align direction, plus damping) produce flocking nobody explicitly programmed — emergence. You design the rules, the system designs the motion. This is the generative mindset: author the system, curate the output.

choices: More code always means more interesting output
Constrain the parameter space tightly, then explore it systematically (grid search the seeds/params)
Only ever run it once
Complexity comes from large file sizes
evidence: sketch.js
// 40 parameters; every run looks either boring or broken
scenarios.hint: With 40 free parameters, what fraction of the space is actually good — and how do you find it?
scenarios.prompt: How do you find the good region of a huge parameter space?
scenarios.situation: 40 parameters; most runs are boring or broken; occasionally one is magic.
scenarios.title: The parameter desert
scenarios.why: Constrain ruthlessly (fewer, well-ranged parameters), then explore systematically: render contact sheets across seeds and key params, and keep what sings. Generative art is search — the artist's taste is the fitness function. Forty unconstrained parameters is a desert; eight tuned ones with good ranges is a garden.

choices: Export at screen resolution; it's fine
Render at high resolution with pixelDensity() / large offscreen buffers, using fixed seeds so the export matches the preview
Trace it by hand
Screenshots are the professional standard
evidence: brief.txt
Gallery wants a 48-inch print of the piece. Screen preview: 800px.
scenarios.hint: The piece is code, not pixels — what does that imply about resolution?
scenarios.prompt: How do you deliver a 48-inch print from an 800px preview?
scenarios.situation: A gallery wants a large-format print of your generative piece.
scenarios.title: The gallery export
scenarios.why: Re-render from the same seed at print resolution: pixelDensity(4), or a large createGraphics buffer, or scale all units. Because the artwork is a deterministic function of (seed, params), resolution is just a render setting — the unique advantage of code art over raster painting. Fixed seeds make the export match the approved preview exactly.

scenarios.title: The Disappearing Masterpiece
scenarios.situation: Your generative piece uses Math.random() everywhere. A collector saw a beautiful variant at a show, asked for a print of exactly that frame, and you cannot reproduce it. You also cannot recreate the variant a gallery asked about after you rebooted the machine.
scenarios.prompt: What change makes any variant reproducible on demand?
choices: Take a screenshot of every frame so you always have a record of what appeared
Replace Math.random() with a seeded PRNG (e.g., mulberry32) and record the seed for each notable variant; re-running with the same seed reproduces it exactly
Increase the randomness by mixing in timestamps so each run is unique and valuable
Save the particle positions to a file at the end of each run
scenarios.why: A seeded PRNG produces a deterministic sequence from its seed, so seed + code = exact reproduction. This is the foundation of generative editioning: artists mint or print specific seeds. Screenshots capture one frame but cannot regenerate the system; Math.random() is unseedable by design.
scenarios.hint: What is the one input that, combined with your code, determines every 'random' choice?
objectives: Use seeded randomness for reproducible generative work
evidence: Explain how a seed lets you re-mint an exact variant

scenarios.title: Parameter Space That Fights Back
scenarios.situation: Your flow-field piece has 14 parameters (noise scale, octaves, line length, hue range, etc.). Tweaking them live gives you either mud or magic with no middle ground, and clients keep asking for 'the same but calmer' — a request you cannot translate into parameter changes reliably.
scenarios.prompt: How should you restructure the parameter space so the work becomes steerable?
choices: Expose all 14 parameters as sliders in the UI so nothing is hidden from the user
Build a small set of high-level controls (energy, calm, density, palette) that each drive several low-level parameters through curated mappings, and define presets from known-good combinations
Randomize parameters on a timer so the piece explores the space by itself
Reduce to 3 parameters by deleting the rest, accepting less variety
scenarios.why: Raw low-level parameters interact non-linearly, which is why 'calmer' is untranslatable. A macro-control layer maps human language to coordinated parameter moves (e.g., 'calm' lowers speed, narrows hue range, reduces octaves), and presets anchor exploration to known-good regions. The full set stays for experts.
scenarios.hint: The client speaks in adjectives, your system speaks in numbers — where should the translation happen?
objectives: Design macro-controls and presets over raw parameter spaces
evidence: Map the adjective 'calmer' to three coordinated parameter changes

choices: if (mouseX > 0) fill(red);
Map it: let hue = map(mouseX, 0, width, 0, 360); — full sweep across the canvas
Use mouseX directly as the hue
Mouse can't drive color smoothly

// want: moving the mouse left-right sweeps the background through the rainbow
scenarios.hint: mouseX lives in [0, width]; hue wants [0, 360] — what function translates ranges?

scenarios.situation: Moving the mouse left to right should sweep the background through the full rainbow.
scenarios.title: The rainbow mouse
scenarios.why: map(mouseX, 0, width, 0, 360) translates the mouse range into hue degrees — left edge red, right edge back to red. map() is the universal adapter between input ranges and visual ranges. Direct use of mouseX as hue only works if width happens to be 360.

choices: They're identical; use either
mousePressed() fires once per click (event); checking mouseIsPressed in draw() is true for every frame the button is held
mouseIsPressed is deprecated

evidence: sketch.js

scenarios.prompt: Each click should spawn exactly one firework. Which approach?

scenarios.why: mousePressed() is an event: it fires once per click. mouseIsPressed is state: true for every frame the button stays down (dozens of frames per click). Events for discrete actions (spawn, toggle), polling for continuous ones (dragging, holding). Mixing them up is the classic interaction bug.

choices: Poll keyIsPressed in draw() for everything

scenarios.prompt: How do you make the interaction work on phones?
scenarios.situation: A gallery piece must run on visitors' phones.
scenarios.title: The touch gap
scenarios.why: Implement touchStarted()/touchMoved() alongside (or instead of) mouse handlers, and return false to stop the browser scrolling/zooming over your canvas. mousePressed sometimes fires on mobile, but unreliably — dedicated touch handlers are the robust path. Test on a real phone; simulators lie about touch.

choices: One giant draw() with flags everywhere
A state variable (e.g., mode = 'attract' | 'play' | 'rest') with a switch in draw() and transitions on events/timeout
Separate HTML pages per scene
States are overengineering
evidence: sketch.js
// installation: attract loop -> interactive play -> rest screen, cycling
scenarios.hint: Three behaviors, clean transitions — what pattern keeps them from tangling?
scenarios.prompt: How do you structure the installation's three modes?
scenarios.situation: An installation cycles: attract loop, interactive play, rest screen.
scenarios.title: The mode machine
scenarios.why: A mode variable with a switch in draw() — each case self-contained, transitions triggered by events or timers. States keep behaviors from tangling into flag spaghetti, and adding a fourth mode later is trivial. Almost every interactive installation is a small state machine wearing an art costume.

scenarios.title: The Touch That Never Lands
scenarios.situation: Your interactive piece responds to pointer movement, but on touchscreens visitors complain it feels 'sticky' — the visuals lag behind their finger, and quick flicks get ignored entirely. Mouse testing on your laptop felt fine.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause, and the correct fix?
choices: Touch devices are slower, so reduce the particle count by half for mobile browsers
Increase the canvas size so there is more area for the finger to move in
The code listens to mousemove only; add pointer events (pointermove/pointerdown) with touch-action: none, and sample velocity between events instead of relying on per-frame positions
Debounce the touch handler so it fires less often and the browser can keep up
scenarios.why: mousemove does not fire for touches; Pointer Events unify mouse/touch/pen. touch-action: none stops the browser from hijacking gestures for scroll/zoom, which is the real source of 'stickiness'. Sampling velocity between events (not just positions per frame) makes flicks register even at low event rates.
scenarios.hint: Before performance, check whether the input events you need are even firing on a touchscreen.
objectives: Implement responsive touch interaction with Pointer Events
evidence: List the two code changes needed for touch parity with mouse

scenarios.title: Interaction Without Instruction
scenarios.situation: At the gallery opening, visitors stand in front of your interactive projection and do nothing — they don't realize it's interactive. The few who wave at it get no feedback, because the camera tracks full-body motion but the piece only responds to fast movement.
scenarios.prompt: What design change makes the piece discoverable and rewarding within the first 10 seconds?
choices: Add a text overlay explaining the controls in three languages
Increase the camera resolution so tracking is more accurate
Add an attract mode that hints at interaction (e.g., a ripple that follows the nearest person) and lower the response threshold so subtle movement produces immediate, obvious feedback
Make the piece fully autonomous and remove interactivity, since visitors are passive
scenarios.why: Discoverability beats documentation in public space: an attract loop that reacts to presence teaches the interaction without words, and a sensitive threshold guarantees the first move is rewarded. Text overlays get ignored, and accuracy fixes don't help if nobody tries. The feedback must be instant and proportional.
scenarios.hint: What does a visitor learn in the first 3 seconds — and does anything in the piece teach them?
objectives: Design discoverable interaction with attract modes and feedback thresholds
evidence: Describe an attract-mode behavior that teaches interactivity without text

choices: Multiply the sensor value by 2 and hope
map(sensor, 0, 1023, 20, 400): translate the 10-bit range into a radius range
Use the raw value as the radius
Sensors can't drive visuals
evidence: arduino.txt
Sensor reads 0-1023. Want: circle radius 20-400 px.
scenarios.hint: map() takes five arguments — value, then the input range, then the output range. What are they here?
scenarios.prompt: How do you convert the sensor reading into a radius?
scenarios.situation: A 10-bit sensor (0–1023) should drive a circle's radius (20–400 px).
scenarios.title: The sensor mapping
scenarios.why: map(sensor, 0, 1023, 20, 400) linearly translates ranges — the single most-used function in interactive art. It also clamps nothing by default (values outside map outside — constrain() if needed) and works in reverse (map(x, 0, 1023, 400, 20) inverts). Range translation is the whole job of physical computing.

choices: x = r * a; y = r * a;
x = cx + r * cos(a); y = cy + r * sin(a); — with a in radians
x = cx + a; y = cy + a;
Circles can't be parametric
evidence: sketch.js
// want: 12 dots evenly spaced on a circle of radius 150
scenarios.hint: A point on a circle is an angle plus a radius — how do sine and cosine split those into x and y?
scenarios.prompt: How do you place 12 dots evenly on a circle?
scenarios.situation: Twelve dots, evenly spaced, on a circle of radius 150 centered at (cx, cy).
scenarios.title: The polar layout
scenarios.why: For i in 0..11: a = i * TWO_PI / 12; x = cx + 150*cos(a); y = cy + 150*sin(a). Polar coordinates (angle, radius) are the natural language of circular layouts — orbits, radial menus, flower petals, clock faces. TWO_PI/12 spaces them evenly; cos/sin project onto x/y.

choices: rotate() takes degrees; the code is fine
Multiply by 100 to fix it
rotate() expects radians: rotate(radians(45)) or angleMode(DEGREES) — 45 radians spins ~7 full turns
Use rotateX instead
evidence: sketch.js
rotate(45);  // expected: tilt 45 degrees. Got: wild spinning.
scenarios.hint: 45 of what? p5.js trig functions default to one angular unit — which?
scenarios.prompt: Why does rotate(45) spin wildly instead of tilting 45°?
scenarios.situation: rotate(45) was meant to tilt 45 degrees but produces wild spinning.
scenarios.title: The radian trap
scenarios.why: p5.js trig defaults to radians: 45 radians ≈ 7.16 full rotations. Fix with rotate(radians(45)) or angleMode(DEGREES) in setup(). This is the most common math bug in creative coding — always check which unit a function expects before assuming degrees.

choices: lerpColor(colorA, colorB, t) with t swept 0→1 across the shape
Alternate fill() calls randomly
Use two canvases
Gradients are impossible in p5.js
evidence: sketch.js
// want: smooth vertical gradient from deep blue to warm orange
scenarios.hint: A gradient is just many small steps — what interpolates between two colors?
scenarios.prompt: How do you paint the gradient?
scenarios.situation: A smooth vertical gradient from deep blue to warm orange.
scenarios.title: The gradient blend
scenarios.why: Loop over rows: t = y / height; stroke(lerpColor(blue, orange, t)); line across. lerpColor interpolates every channel by t — the color twin of lerp(). In HSB mode the blend travels through hue space (often prettier); in RGB it can pass through muddy middles. Gradients are interpolation made visible.

choices: Check every pair with nested ifs on raw coordinates
dist(x1, y1, x2, y2) < threshold — Euclidean distance, one call
Estimate with x-distance only
Proximity can't be computed per frame
evidence: sketch.js
// 200 particles; nearby pairs should connect with lines
scenarios.hint: 'Nearby' is a distance — what function computes it directly?
scenarios.prompt: How do you find nearby particle pairs?
scenarios.situation: 200 particles; pairs closer than 60px should be connected with lines.
scenarios.title: The proximity lines
scenarios.why: if (dist(a.x, a.y, b.x, b.y) < 60) line(...). dist() is Euclidean distance in one call — the basis of connection effects, repulsion, attraction, and collision. (At 200 particles, all-pairs is 20k checks/frame — fine; at 2000, you'd want spatial hashing. Know your n².)

choices: Place seeds randomly; nature is random
Use the golden angle 137.5°: each seed at angle i*137.5°, radius growing with sqrt(i) — optimal packing, zero overlap
Space them evenly at 180°
Packing doesn't matter visually
evidence: sketch.js
// want: a sunflower head of 500 seeds, perfectly packed
scenarios.hint: 137.5° is 360°/φ² — the most irrational turn. Why would irrationality pack best?
scenarios.prompt: How do you pack 500 seeds like a sunflower?
scenarios.situation: A sunflower head: 500 seeds, perfectly packed, no overlaps, no gaps.
scenarios.title: The golden angle
scenarios.why: Angle = i × 137.5°, radius = c × √i. The golden angle (360°/φ²) is the 'most irrational' turn, so no seed ever lines up behind another — optimal packing emerges from one multiplication. Radius grows with √i so area per seed stays constant. This is phyllotaxis: mathematics' most beautiful generative algorithm, running in every sunflower.

scenarios.title: The Orbit That Drifts
scenarios.situation: You coded an orbiting particle with x = cx + cos(angle)*r, y = cy + sin(angle)*r, incrementing angle each frame. Over minutes, the orbit slowly drifts off-center and the trail becomes an ellipse-ish smear instead of a clean circle.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely mathematical cause, and the fix?
choices: cos and sin are approximations, so you should use a lookup table for exact values
The canvas is not square, so circles render as ellipses — force a square aspect ratio
requestAnimationFrame skips frames under load, stretching the orbit
Floating-point accumulation in the ever-growing angle loses precision; wrap the angle with modulo 2*PI each frame (or compute angle from elapsed time)
scenarios.why: An angle that grows unboundedly accumulates floating-point error, and cos/sin of huge arguments lose precision — the classic drift. Wrapping angle modulo TAU keeps the argument small and exact. Computing angle = t * speed from elapsed time additionally makes the orbit deterministic and pause-safe.
scenarios.hint: What happens to floating-point precision as your angle variable grows into the thousands?
objectives: Prevent floating-point drift in parametric motion
evidence: Name two ways to keep a parametric angle numerically stable

scenarios.title: Mapping Sensor Chaos to Beauty
scenarios.situation: Your installation maps a depth-camera reading (raw values 0–4000, noisy, with occasional spikes to 4000 when nobody is present) to the hue of a particle system (0–360). Direct linear mapping makes the colors flicker wildly and jump to red whenever the sensor glitches.
scenarios.prompt: What mapping pipeline produces stable, beautiful output from this noisy sensor?
choices: Map 0–4000 directly to 0–360 with a linear function and clamp the result
Smooth the input (exponential moving average), reject or clamp spike outliers, map a calibrated active range (e.g., 300–2500) to hue with an easing curve, and slew-rate-limit the output
Average the hue over 60 frames so the flicker cancels out
Switch the sensor to a binary mode (person/no person) and animate hue on a timer
scenarios.why: Raw sensor data needs conditioning: smoothing kills jitter, outlier rejection kills spikes, mapping only the calibrated active range uses the full hue range for real presence, an easing curve makes motion feel natural, and slew limiting prevents any remaining jump from reaching the visuals. Linear direct mapping passes every defect straight through.
scenarios.hint: The sensor gives you truth plus three kinds of lies — which stage of the pipeline handles each?
objectives: Build a sensor-conditioning pipeline: smooth, reject, calibrate, ease, limit
evidence: Order the five stages of a robust sensor-to-visual mapping

choices: Buy a faster laptop
Reduce per-frame work: fewer objects, noStroke() where possible, avoid allocations in draw(), use buffers for static layers
Increase frameRate(120)
Add more visual effects
evidence: perf.txt
3000 particles with shadows and blur: 9 fps. Target: 60.
scenarios.hint: Profile the cost per particle — which operations are the most expensive per frame?
scenarios.prompt: How do you get from 9 fps to 60?
scenarios.situation: 3000 particles with per-particle shadows and blur run at 9 fps.
scenarios.title: The frame-rate rescue
scenarios.why: Kill the expensive per-frame ops first: shadows/blur are brutally costly — fake them with gradients or drop them. Then: fewer objects, noStroke(), no per-frame allocations (GC pauses), static layers into buffers. Creative-coding performance is almost always about doing less per frame, not faster hardware.

choices: Fixed 1920×1080 canvas; everyone has that
createCanvas(windowWidth, windowHeight), derive all layout from width/height, handle windowResized()
Detect the device brand and hardcode
One canvas size per visitor, chosen at random
evidence: brief.txt
Piece shown on phones, laptops, and a 4K gallery wall.
scenarios.hint: You can't know the screen — so what must the layout be a function of?
scenarios.prompt: How do you make one piece work on phones and a 4K wall?
scenarios.situation: The piece shows on phones, laptops, and a 4K gallery wall.
scenarios.title: The every-screen piece
scenarios.why: Fullscreen canvas + relative layout (positions as fractions of width/height) + windowResized() handler. The piece becomes a function of the viewport, not a fixed image. Test the extremes: tiny phones expose cramped UI, huge walls expose low particle counts. Responsive generative art is layout-as-function.

choices: Motion is the art; accessibility doesn't apply
Add a prefers-reduced-motion check: offer a static or gentle mode when the user requests reduced motion
Remove all motion for everyone
Accessibility is the venue's problem
evidence: a11y.txt
Piece: rapid flashing particles. Visitor reports vestibular discomfort.
scenarios.hint: Rapid flashing can harm — and operating systems broadcast the user's motion preference. What should the piece do with it?
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle motion sensitivity?
scenarios.situation: Rapid flashing particles cause a visitor vestibular discomfort.
scenarios.title: The reduced-motion mode
scenarios.why: Check matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)') and offer a calm alternative: static composition, slow drift, no flashing. Rapid strobing can trigger seizures — this is safety, not taste. The best pieces treat the gentle mode as a first-class composition, not a degraded fallback.

choices: Leave the browser chrome visible; it's authentic
Fullscreen presentation: fullscreen(true) on interaction, noCursor(), hide UI chrome — the piece fills the world
Present from the code editor
Read the code aloud as the presentation
evidence: venue.txt
Gallery opening: piece projected 12 feet wide, artist's laptop visible.
scenarios.hint: The audience came for the art, not the IDE — what disappears between studio and stage?
scenarios.prompt: How do you present the piece at the opening?
scenarios.situation: Gallery opening, 12-foot projection, your laptop and browser chrome visible.
scenarios.title: The stage mode
scenarios.why: fullscreen(true) (triggered by a click, per browser policy), noCursor(), all UI hidden — the work fills the visual field with nothing between it and the viewer. Studio chrome (editors, consoles, cursors) breaks the spell. Present like a projectionist, not a programmer: the piece is the performance.

choices: The final PNG is enough
Document seeds, parameter ranges, and the code version — future-you (or a collector) can regenerate any variation exactly
Nobody needs to reproduce art
Delete old versions to stay clean
evidence: archive.txt
2 years later: which seed made the sold piece? Unknown.
scenarios.hint: The artwork is a function of (code, seed, params) — which of those are you currently throwing away?
scenarios.prompt: How do you archive a generative practice?
scenarios.situation: Two years later, nobody knows which seed produced the sold piece.
scenarios.title: The lost seed
scenarios.why: Version the code (git), log seeds and parameter sets per output, keep contact sheets. A generative practice is a laboratory notebook as much as a portfolio: every interesting output should be regenerable. The PNG is the artifact; the (code, seed, params) triple is the artwork.

choices: Dump every sketch ever made, uncurated
Curate 8-12 strong pieces with process: seeds, parameter studies, and a short statement of the system behind each
Only show the code, not the output
A portfolio is unnecessary for generative artists
evidence: portfolio.txt
200 sketches, wildly varying quality, no statements.
scenarios.hint: A portfolio is an argument about your practice — what is the argument here?
scenarios.prompt: How do you turn 200 sketches into a portfolio?
scenarios.situation: 200 sketches of varying quality, no statements, no curation.
scenarios.title: The curated portfolio
scenarios.why: Select 8–12 pieces that argue something about your practice, each with the system behind it (rules, parameters, seeds) and process artifacts (studies, failures). Curators and clients hire the thinking, not just the images. Two hundred uncurated sketches say 'prolific'; twelve argued pieces say 'artist.'

scenarios.title: The Portfolio That Loads Forever
scenarios.situation: Your portfolio page embeds five live canvas pieces, each running its own animation loop. On your machine it's fine, but visitors on laptops report the fan spinning up, the page stuttering, and one piece freezing the whole tab when they scroll past it.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct performance strategy for a portfolio of live pieces?
choices: Combine all five pieces into one canvas and one animation loop to reduce overhead
Lazy-start each piece only when it scrolls into view (IntersectionObserver), pause offscreen pieces, render thumbnails or poster frames otherwise, and cap pixel ratio on small canvases
Reduce each piece to 30fps so the total load matches a single 60fps loop
Convert the pieces to video files and embed those instead of live code
scenarios.why: Five always-on WebGL/canvas loops compete for GPU and main-thread time; most are offscreen anyway. IntersectionObserver-gated start/stop means only visible work runs, poster frames give instant perceived load, and pixel-ratio caps bound the fill-rate cost. Merging canvases doesn't remove the offscreen waste.
scenarios.hint: How many of the five pieces is the visitor actually looking at at any moment?
objectives: Apply lazy lifecycle management to embedded live pieces
evidence: Name the browser API that detects when a piece enters the viewport

scenarios.title: Documenting the Ephemeral
scenarios.situation: Your best piece is interactive and generative — no two visits are alike. Your portfolio currently shows a single screenshot, and curators keep passing because they 'can't tell what it does'. A 10-minute screen recording you tried felt dead without the interaction.
scenarios.prompt: What documentation best represents an interactive generative piece to curators?
choices: A 60–90 second edited video: 10 seconds of attract mode, then hands visibly interacting (cursor or body), showing range of outcomes, ending on the title card — plus 3 stills of distinct states
A full uncut 10-minute screen capture so nothing is hidden
A written artist statement describing the interaction in detail, with the single screenshot
Only stills, since video compresses the colors badly
scenarios.why: Curators decide in about a minute: the video must show the interaction loop (input → response) quickly, prove range (multiple states), and be short enough to actually watch. Visible hands/body teach the interaction mode; stills of distinct states show generative range for print/press use. Uncut video and text-only both fail the attention test.
scenarios.hint: What does the curator need to believe in the first 20 seconds — and what proves it?
objectives: Document interactive work with short interaction-first video
evidence: Outline the three beats of a 60-second documentation video

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Creative Code as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The Canvas & Drawing Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Canvas & Drawing is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Canvas & Drawing?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Canvas & Drawing issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Canvas & Drawing is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Canvas & Drawing supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Canvas & Drawing failure in Creative Code.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Canvas & Drawing
evidence: System Status
All Canvas & Drawing components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
User Report
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

scenarios.title: Render Pipeline Anatomy: The Missing Frame
scenarios.situation: Your p5.js sketch draws 2,000 agents with per-agent shadowBlur, and the frame rate collapses to 12fps. The profiler shows most time in the browser's paint step, not your JavaScript. A friend suggests 'just use WebGL', but you want to understand the actual bottleneck first.
scenarios.prompt: Trace the frame through the pipeline — where is the time actually going, and what is the minimal fix?
choices: The bottleneck is JavaScript math; move the agent math into a Web Worker
The canvas is too large; shrink it to 400x300

shadowBlur forces the browser to rasterize each shape through an expensive offscreen blur pass per draw call — 2,000 shadow draws means 2,000 blur rasterizations; bake the glow into a pre-rendered sprite and drawImage it instead
requestAnimationFrame is throttled; switch to setInterval for more frames
scenarios.why: Trace the journey: JS issues draw calls → canvas 2D state changes → the browser rasterizes. shadowBlur is not a cheap flag — each shadowed draw triggers a full blur of the shape's alpha mask on the CPU rasterizer. Pre-rendering one glowing sprite and stamping it with drawImage collapses 2,000 blur passes into 2,000 cheap blits. The JS math was never the bottleneck; the profiler's paint-step dominance is the evidence.
scenarios.hint: Follow the frame: your code ends, then what does the browser do with 2,000 shadowed shapes?
objectives: Trace a frame through the 2D canvas render pipeline
Identify rasterization bottlenecks vs JS bottlenecks
evidence: State which pipeline stage (JS / rasterize / composite) dominates, with profiler evidence

scenarios.title: Frame Loop Anatomy: The Spiral of Death
scenarios.situation: Your physics-based piece uses a fixed timestep accumulator: while (acc >= step) { simulate(step); acc -= step; }. On a slow machine, the tab freezes entirely — the animation never catches up, and the page becomes unresponsive until the browser kills it.
scenarios.prompt: What is happening inside the loop, and how do you fix it without breaking determinism?
choices: The accumulator lets the simulation run unlimited catch-up steps per frame — on a slow machine each frame adds more debt than it clears, so the while loop never exits; clamp the maximum steps per frame (e.g., 5) and let the simulation slow down instead of spiral
Remove the accumulator and simulate with raw delta time
Increase the step size so fewer steps are needed per frame
Run the simulation in a Web Worker so the main thread stays responsive
scenarios.why: Trace it: frame takes 100ms, acc grows by 100ms of debt, but the machine can only simulate 40ms per frame — debt grows forever and the while loop consumes the whole frame budget: the spiral of death. Clamping steps per frame bounds the work; the piece runs in slow motion on weak machines instead of freezing, and determinism is preserved because steps stay fixed-size.
scenarios.hint: What happens to the accumulator when one frame's debt exceeds what the machine can simulate in one frame?
objectives: Explain the fixed-timestep spiral of death
Apply step clamping as the standard guard
evidence: Show the accumulator math that proves debt grows unboundedly

scenarios.title: Audio Signal Chain: The Latency Ghost
scenarios.situation: Your audio-reactive visuals lag the beat by a noticeable fraction of a second. The chain is: microphone → AnalyserNode → requestAnimationFrame read → draw. You lowered the FFT size and it barely helped. The beat still lands late.
scenarios.prompt: Trace the signal end to end — which stage actually owns the latency?
choices: The FFT size dominates latency, so keep lowering it until the lag disappears

The chain has three latencies: hardware/input buffer latency (OS audio stack), AnalyserNode smoothing (timeConstant averages across frames), and the rAF-to-draw delay (visuals render up to a frame after the read); the fix is minimizing smoothingTimeConstant, reading the analyser as late as possible in the frame, and accepting that OS input latency is a floor you measure, not eliminate
requestAnimationFrame is the problem; poll the analyser in a tight setInterval loop instead
The microphone is low quality; use a line-in source
scenarios.why: Trace the signal: sound → OS capture buffer (10–50ms floor) → AnalyserNode's internal smoothing (timeConstant blends history; the default 0.8 smears attacks) → your rAF callback reads, then the draw happens up to 16ms later. FFT size affects frequency resolution, barely latency. The honest fix: zero the smoothing for transient response, read late in the frame, and measure the floor — then design visuals that anticipate the beat rather than chase it.
scenarios.hint: List every buffer and averaging stage between the sound wave and the pixel — which ones did you actually change?
objectives: Trace latency through an audio-reactive signal chain
Distinguish reducible latency from floor latency
evidence: Name the three latency stages and which one is a fixed floor

scenarios.title: Shader GPU Pipeline: The Banding Mystery
scenarios.situation: Your fragment shader renders a smooth radial gradient, but on screen you see distinct concentric bands instead of a smooth falloff. The math is continuous — distance-based mix with no quantization. It looks fine in your head but banded on the monitor.
scenarios.prompt: Trace the value from shader to eye — where does the banding enter?
choices: The GPU computes in low precision by default; add 'precision highp float' to fix it
The monitor is broken; test on another display

The shader outputs 8 bits per channel to the default framebuffer — a smooth gradient across 256 levels is too coarse for the eye to see as continuous; add dithering (ordered or blue-noise) in the shader to break bands, or render to a float target
Banding comes from the distance function; replace it with a noise-based falloff
scenarios.why: Trace it: shader computes smooth float → written to an 8-bit-per-channel framebuffer (256 steps) → the eye is exquisitely sensitive to Mach bands at those steps. highp doesn't help because the quantization happens at framebuffer write, not in ALU precision. Dithering adds sub-LSB noise that the eye averages into perceived smoothness — the standard production fix, costing almost nothing.
scenarios.hint: Your math is continuous, but what is the bit depth of the surface it lands on?
objectives: Trace precision loss from shader math to framebuffer
Apply dithering as the standard banding fix
evidence: Explain why highp precision does not fix gradient banding

scenarios.title: Interaction Event Flow: The Phantom Double-Tap
scenarios.situation: On the gallery touchscreen, every tap on your piece triggers the action twice — shapes spawn in pairs. Your handler is a single 'click' listener. It works perfectly with a mouse in the studio.
scenarios.prompt: Trace the touch through the browser's event system — what produces the double fire?
choices: The touchscreen hardware sends duplicate signals; debounce the handler with a 300ms timer
Two fingers are touching; require single-touch tracking
The handler is registered twice because the script loads twice

The browser synthesizes a compatibility mouse/click event ~300ms after the touch events (touchstart/touchend → mouseover/mousemove/mousedown/mouseup/click); if you listen to both touch and click (or a library does), the action fires twice — use Pointer Events exclusively with touch-action: none
scenarios.why: Trace the flow: touchstart → touchend → the browser waits ~300ms (legacy double-tap-zoom detection) → fires synthetic mouse events including click. A 'click' listener alone fires once — the doubling means something also listens to touch/pointer, or a framework normalizes both. Pointer Events give one unified stream; touch-action: none removes the 300ms delay and the zoom gesture, killing both the lag and the phantom.
scenarios.hint: What does the browser do 300ms after a touch ends, and why does that legacy behavior exist?
objectives: Trace touch input through the browser's compatibility event synthesis
Unify input handling with Pointer Events
evidence: List the synthetic events the browser fires after touchend

scenarios.title: Installation Signal Path: The Midnight Freeze
scenarios.situation: Your gallery installation — depth camera → PC → projector — runs fine all day but freezes every night around 2 AM, recovering by morning. Logs show the app alive but the camera feed timestamp stalls. The venue swears nothing changes overnight.
scenarios.prompt: Trace the signal path — which component is the likely culprit, and what evidence confirms it?
choices: The PC is overheating; add cooling and the freezes will stop

Trace the path: camera USB → driver → app → GPU → projector. The 2 AM pattern matches the venue's automated systems — likely USB power management suspending the port, or a nightly backup/AV scan starving the driver; evidence is Windows Event Log entries for USB suspend at 2 AM and the camera timestamp (not app timestamp) stalling, proving the break is upstream of your code
Your code has a memory leak that takes ~12 hours to crash the feed
The projector overheats and stops accepting signal overnight
scenarios.why: The camera timestamp stalling while the app stays alive localizes the break: upstream of your code, at the camera/driver boundary — your code is innocent. The clockwork 2 AM timing points at scheduled venue systems, not thermals or leaks (which drift). USB selective suspend is the classic: the OS parks the port to save power. Evidence chain — event log + upstream timestamp — is the systems-thinking move: localize by timestamps, then confirm with logs.
scenarios.hint: Two timestamps exist: the camera's and your app's. Which one stalled, and what does that prove about where the break is?
objectives: Localize installation failures using timestamp evidence
Distinguish scheduled-system causes from code causes
evidence: State which log entry would confirm USB suspend vs a memory leak
