scenarios.title: The Portfolio Review
scenarios.situation: You have 14 pieces for a creative technologist application. Three are strong, five are good, four are mediocre, two are broken demos. The deadline is tomorrow.
scenarios.prompt: What do you submit?
choices: All 14 — volume shows range and productivity
The 8 strong/good pieces, each with process shots and code links; cut the mediocre and broken without mercy. Add the one-paragraph story per piece tonight
Only the 3 strong pieces — perfection over quantity
The 3 strong + fix the 2 broken demos overnight
scenarios.why: Eight curated pieces with stories and process proof beat fourteen mixed with dead weight: reviewers judge your taste by your weakest included piece. Three is too few to show range; fixing broken demos overnight risks submitting broken-plus-rushed. The curation — what you chose to cut — is itself the skill being evaluated. Write the stories tonight; they convert 'nice visuals' into 'hired'.
scenarios.hint: What does your weakest included piece say about your judgment?
evidence: Pieces
14 total: 3 strong, 5 good, 4 mediocre, 2 broken
Deadline
Tomorrow, 9 AM. Stories not yet written.

scenarios.title: The Portfolio Cut
scenarios.situation: You have 23 pieces from three years of work. A curator friend says your portfolio 'has no point of view' — strong pieces drown among student exercises and client compromises. You need to cut to 8 for a festival application due Friday.
scenarios.prompt: What selection principle produces the strongest 8-piece portfolio?
choices: Select for a coherent thesis: 8 pieces that together argue one idea about your practice (e.g., 'systems that listen'), cutting anything that doesn't serve it even if it's technically impressive
Pick your 8 personal favorites — passion reads through the screen
Pick the 8 most technically complex pieces to prove your skills
Include one piece from every year to show growth over time
scenarios.why: Curators remember arguments, not inventories. A thesis-driven selection turns 8 pieces into one memorable statement, and the cuts themselves sharpen it — the impressive-but-off-thesis piece actively dilutes the message. Favorites and complexity are artist-centered criteria; the portfolio is a reader-centered document.
scenarios.hint: After viewing, what single sentence should the curator be able to say about your work?
objectives: Curate a portfolio around a thesis, not a chronology
evidence: Write the one-sentence thesis your 8 pieces argue

scenarios.title: Documentation That Sells
scenarios.situation: A venue wants to book your interactive wall but needs to 'see how audiences react' before committing. You have beautiful stills, a 30-second teaser, and raw 20-minute footage from the last show with great crowd moments buried inside.
scenarios.prompt: What documentation package do you send, and why?
choices: The stills plus the teaser — short and professional
The full 20-minute raw footage so they see everything honestly

A 2-minute edit built for the booker: 15s of the piece alone, 60s of diverse visitors interacting (kids, elders, hesitant-to-engaged arcs), 30s of the room's energy, 15s title card with specs — plus a one-page tech rider
Stills only, since video never captures the real feeling
scenarios.why: The booker is buying audience reaction, not your art — the edit must prove strangers engage, with arc (hesitant → delighted) as the persuasion. The tech rider answers their next question (power, space, setup time) before they ask, removing friction. Raw footage buries the proof; stills can't show interaction at all.
scenarios.hint: Whose decision are you informing, and what risk are they trying to retire?
objectives: Build booker-facing documentation: proof of engagement + tech rider
evidence: List the four beats of the 2-minute booker edit

scenarios.title: Pricing the Commission
scenarios.situation: A brand offers $8,000 for a 3-month interactive installation. Your last similar piece took 6 weeks of build plus 2 weeks on-site, and you burned out doing it solo. They want exclusivity in their sector and full source code handover.
scenarios.prompt: How should you respond to make this sustainable?
choices: Accept — $8,000 is good money and the exposure will lead to more work
Accept but quietly reuse code from other projects to save time

Counter with an itemized quote: build fee covering 8 weeks at your day rate, on-site days billed separately, exclusivity and source handover as priced add-ons, and a maintenance retainer — then negotiate from the itemized total, not the $8,000 anchor
Decline all brand work on principle and wait for art funding
scenarios.why: Itemization moves negotiation from their anchor ($8,000) to your costs (8 weeks labor + site time + IP terms). Exclusivity and source handover are assets with real value — giving them away free is how artists subsidize brands. The burnout came from unbilled scope; priced line items make scope visible and negotiable.
scenarios.hint: What did the last piece actually cost you in weeks — and which parts of their ask are assets, not favors?
objectives: Price commissions with itemized quotes and IP add-ons
evidence: Name three line items that must appear in any installation quote

scenarios.title: The Difficult Client Email
scenarios.situation: Mid-build, the client asks for 'just one more feature' — real-time social media integration — that would add two weeks and a moderation liability. The contract has a vague 'reasonable revisions' clause. You need to say no without losing the client.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct response structure?
choices: Say yes to keep them happy, then absorb the extra work quietly
Refuse outright, citing the contract's scope section

Acknowledge the idea's appeal, name the concrete cost (2 weeks, moderation risk, timeline impact on their launch date), offer it as a priced Phase 2 after launch, and ask which launch-date trade-off they prefer — all in writing
Agree verbally but deprioritize it, hoping they forget
scenarios.why: The structure — validate, cost, reframe as Phase 2, force the trade-off choice — keeps the relationship while making scope real. 'Reasonable revisions' is vague, so you replace vibes with specifics: dates and dollars. In writing, because verbal scope agreements evaporate. Absorbing it teaches the client that scope is free.
scenarios.hint: Who should choose between the feature and the launch date — and where should that choice live?
objectives: Deflect scope creep with costed Phase-2 reframing
evidence: Draft the one paragraph that names cost and offers Phase 2

scenarios.title: Festival Application Triage
scenarios.situation: You have one weekend to apply to three festivals. Festival A is prestigious but wants a large-scale outdoor piece you don't have. Festival B fits your existing interactive wall perfectly but has a $50 fee and 2,000 applicants. Festival C is small, free, local — and its curator already follows your work.
scenarios.prompt: How do you allocate the weekend?
choices: Apply to A with a proposal for a new piece — prestige is worth the stretch
Apply to all three with the same generic statement to maximize chances

Skip A (wrong fit wastes the weekend), craft a tailored B application around the proven wall with strong documentation, and send C a short personal note with the piece link since the curator already knows you
Skip festivals entirely; they never lead to paid work
scenarios.why: Fit beats prestige: A's jury will spot the stretch, and proposing unbuilt large-scale work you can't deliver is a reputation risk. B gets the full effort because the piece is proven and the documentation exists. C gets a light personal touch — warm leads convert cheaply. Generic blasts convert at near-zero in juried contexts.
scenarios.hint: Which application can you make undeniable with work that already exists?
objectives: Triage opportunities by fit and proof, not prestige
evidence: State the go/no-go criterion for proposing unbuilt work

scenarios.title: The Grant Narrative
scenarios.situation: A $15,000 media-arts grant asks for a project description, timeline, budget, and 'public benefit'. Your draft reads like a technical spec — impressive to engineers, opaque to the panel of artists and community members who decide.
scenarios.prompt: How should you rewrite the narrative for the panel?
choices: Add more technical detail to prove you can execute it
Make the project sound bigger and more expensive to justify the $15,000

Lead with the public experience (what a visitor feels in the first 30 seconds), translate the tech into one plain sentence, tie the public benefit to the funder's mission language, and put the technical proof in the timeline/budget where it belongs
Submit the technical spec as-is; panels respect expertise
scenarios.why: Panels fund experiences and missions, not architectures. The 30-second visitor feeling is the hook; the one-sentence tech translation proves feasibility without jargon; mirroring the funder's mission language shows alignment; the timeline and budget carry the execution proof where detail is welcome. Technical specs answer questions the panel isn't asking.
scenarios.hint: What does the panelist need to feel confident about — your code, or the visitor's experience?
objectives: Write funder-facing narratives: experience first, mission-aligned
evidence: Write the one-sentence plain-language version of your technical approach

scenarios.title: The Teaching Offer
scenarios.situation: A university offers you a semester teaching creative coding — good pay, but 12 hours/week of prep and contact time during your peak commission season. You've never taught, and the syllabus is yours to design.
scenarios.prompt: How do you decide, and if you accept, how do you protect your practice?
choices: Decline — teaching always kills studio practice
Accept immediately — academic credibility is priceless
Accept and teach from existing tutorials to minimize prep

Accept only if the numbers work: compute the true hourly rate (prep + contact + grading), require the course to feed your practice (students beta-test your tools, syllabus built around your real workflow), and cap it at one semester with a re-evaluation clause
scenarios.why: The decision is arithmetic plus strategy: true hourly rate (teaching prep is 2-3x contact hours) versus commission income, and the course must be an R&D asset, not a drain — students stress-test your systems, and teaching forces articulation that sharpens your own work. The one-semester cap with re-evaluation prevents drift into a second job you didn't choose.
scenarios.hint: What is the real hourly rate once prep is counted — and what does the classroom give back to the studio?
objectives: Evaluate teaching offers on true rate and practice feedback
evidence: Compute a true hourly rate from a 12h/week teaching load

domains.name: Shaders: GPU Thinking
domains.description: Move pixels on the GPU: the shader mindset, GLSL basics, and effects that make work stand out.

scenarios.title: The Black Screen
scenarios.situation: Your first fragment shader compiles with no errors but renders pure black. The code uses a loop `for (int i = 0; i < u_octaves; i++)` where u_octaves is a uniform.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
choices: The GPU is broken — try another machine
Dynamic loop bounds: GLSL ES requires constant loop bounds on many implementations; a uniform bound fails silently to black. Fix: constant MAX_OCTAVES with `if (i >= u_octaves) break;` inside
The monitor brightness is down
Black is the default — add more code until something appears
scenarios.why: Silent black screens are the shader debugger's nightmare, and dynamic loop bounds are a classic cause: GLSL ES (WebGL/mobile) historically requires loops with constant bounds for unrolling. The uniform bound compiles but produces undefined behavior — usually black. The pattern is constant-maximum with an early break. When a shader goes black with no errors, suspect: loop bounds, precision qualifiers, and uninitialized varyings — in that order.
scenarios.hint: No errors, pure black. What GLSL constraint involves loops and uniforms?
evidence: Code
for (int i = 0; i < u_octaves; i++) { ... fbm octave ... }
Symptom
Compiles clean, renders black on all devices.

scenarios.title: Shader or Canvas?
scenarios.situation: Your new piece needs 50,000 particles with per-particle color blending and a bloom-like glow. Your canvas 2D prototype hits 8fps at 5,000 particles. A colleague says 'just write a shader', but you've never touched GLSL.
scenarios.prompt: When is reaching for a shader the right call versus optimizing canvas 2D?
choices: Always optimize canvas 2D first — shaders are only for 3D work

Use a shader when the work is per-pixel or massively parallel (50k particles, fullscreen effects, blend-heavy compositing) — the GPU does in one pass what canvas 2D does in 50,000 draw calls; keep canvas 2D for UI overlays, text, and simple vector scenes where its API wins
Rewrite everything in shaders immediately, including text rendering and UI
Use CSS filters for the glow and keep the particles on canvas 2D
scenarios.why: The decision is architectural: canvas 2D issues one draw call per shape (CPU-bound), while a fragment shader evaluates per pixel in parallel (GPU-bound). 50k particles × per-particle blending is the textbook GPU workload. But canvas 2D keeps winning where its high-level API matters — text, paths, UI — so the pro move is hybrid: shader for the particle field, canvas 2D for overlays.
scenarios.hint: Count the draw calls in your prototype — what does that number become in a shader?
objectives: Decide between shader and canvas 2D by workload shape
evidence: Name one workload that must stay on canvas 2D in a hybrid piece

scenarios.title: The Performance Cliff
scenarios.situation: Your fullscreen shader runs at 60fps on your desktop GPU but drops to 15fps on the gallery's mini-PC with integrated graphics. The shader does 8 octaves of simplex noise per pixel plus a feedback loop at full 4K resolution.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct performance strategy?
choices: Cut the dominant cost first: render the noise at half or quarter resolution and upscale (noise is low-frequency-friendly), reduce octaves where detail is invisible, and make resolution/noise quality adaptive settings rather than fixed — profile which pass actually dominates before touching anything else
Buy a better GPU for the gallery — the art requires it
Reduce the canvas to 720p permanently for all machines
Remove the feedback loop, since feedback is inherently slow
scenarios.why: Fullscreen 4K × 8 noise octaves = ~66M noise evals/frame; integrated GPUs drown in ALU cost. Noise upscales beautifully (it's smooth by nature), so quarter-res noise + upscale keeps 90% of the look at 1/16th the cost. Adaptive quality settings let the piece degrade gracefully across hardware instead of demanding one GPU. Profile first because the dominant pass is often not the one you suspect.
scenarios.hint: Which is cheaper: computing noise at 4K or at 540p and upscaling — and can you see the difference?
objectives: Optimize shaders with resolution scaling and adaptive quality
evidence: Compute the per-frame noise evaluations at 4K vs quarter-res

scenarios.title: Debugging the Black Screen
scenarios.situation: Your fragment shader compiles with no errors but renders pure black. The vertex shader is a standard fullscreen triangle. You've stared at the math for an hour and it 'should' produce color.
scenarios.prompt: What is the systematic debugging approach?
choices: Bisect visually: output intermediate values as color (e.g., gl_FragColor = vec4(uv, 0, 1) to verify coordinates arrive; then output each computation stage in turn) to find where the signal dies — black screens are almost always a zeroed varying, a bad uniform, or a divide that collapses
Rewrite the shader from scratch — faster than debugging
Increase the brightness multiplier until something appears
Assume the GPU driver is broken and test on another machine
scenarios.why: Shaders have no printf and no breakpoints — visualizing intermediates AS color is the debugger. Outputting uv first separates 'geometry/varyings broken' from 'math broken' in one step; then walk the computation forward until the value dies. Most black screens are a varying that never got set, a uniform defaulting to 0, or a normalization dividing by zero.
scenarios.hint: If you could add one print statement to a shader, what would you print — and what is the visual equivalent?
objectives: Debug shaders by visualizing intermediate values as color
evidence: Name the first diagnostic output to render when facing a black screen

scenarios.title: Post-Processing Chain Order
scenarios.situation: Your piece chains three fullscreen passes: bloom, film grain, and vignette. Currently the order is grain → bloom → vignette, and the result looks wrong — the grain sparkles unnaturally and the bloom looks dirty.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct pass order, and why?
choices: Order doesn't matter for fullscreen passes since they all cover the same pixels
Grain → vignette → bloom, since grain is the subtlest effect
Merge all three into one shader to avoid ordering issues

Bloom → vignette → grain: bloom first so it operates on the clean HDR-ish image, vignette darkens edges before grain so the grain is uniform (grain must be LAST, applied to the final image, or earlier passes will smear/amplify it)
scenarios.why: Pass order is semantic: bloom thresholds bright pixels — grain added before bloom gets thresholded and amplified into sparkle; vignette before grain keeps grain energy uniform across the frame (vignette after grain would darken the grain at edges, looking like dirt). Grain last is the film-industry rule: it's a property of the final image, not the scene.
scenarios.hint: What does bloom do to bright pixels — and what happens if the grain is already there when it looks?
objectives: Order post-processing passes by their semantic dependencies
evidence: Explain why grain must be the final pass

scenarios.title: Portability: WebGL vs Everything
scenarios.situation: Your WebGL2 piece is booked for a festival whose hardware runs an older browser with only WebGL1, and the backup plan is projecting from an iPad. Your shader uses 3D noise textures and integer modulo operations.
scenarios.prompt: What portability decisions should you have made (and can still make)?
choices: Require WebGL2 in the tech rider and hope the festival upgrades
Rewrite the piece in a native app for each device
Drop the noise entirely so the shader is trivially portable

Write to the WebGL1-compatible subset (no integer ops, no 3D textures — emulate with 2D noise or hash-based value noise), feature-detect at runtime with a graceful fallback (reduced effects or a pre-rendered video loop), and test on the actual weakest target device before the show
scenarios.why: Festival hardware is the constraint, not your laptop. GLSL ES 1.0 (WebGL1) lacks integer modulo and 3D samplers, but hash-based noise works everywhere — the visual difference is negligible. A runtime fallback (degraded shader or video loop) beats a black screen when detection fails. The tech rider can request, but the piece must survive the hardware that shows up.
scenarios.hint: What is the oldest GPU in the deployment chain, and which of your shader features does it forbid?
objectives: Write portable shaders targeting the weakest deployment GPU
evidence: Name two WebGL2 features that break on WebGL1 and their workarounds

scenarios.title: The Feedback Loop That Explodes
scenarios.situation: Your feedback shader (previous frame fed back as a texture) looks gorgeous for 30 seconds, then blows out to pure white. You added a 0.99 decay multiply, but it still saturates — just more slowly.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the decay fail, and what is the correct stabilization?
choices: 0.99 is too weak; use 0.5 decay instead
Feedback loops are inherently unstable; remove the feedback

Any feedback gain ≥ 1 in the bright regions compounds: values above 1.0 grow exponentially regardless of the 0.99 factor when the shader adds energy each frame (e.g., additive deposits); the fix is a soft clamp (tone map / smoothstep ceiling) plus ensuring total loop gain < 1, not just a fixed decay
Render at a lower resolution so values can't accumulate as fast
scenarios.why: Decay multiplies the old frame, but if the shader ADDS new energy each frame (deposits, bloom pickup), regions where add > decay grow without bound — 0.99 only slows the explosion. Stability needs loop gain < 1 everywhere: a soft ceiling (e.g., color = 1 - exp(-color)) guarantees bounded output no matter the input, which is why tone mapping is the standard feedback stabilizer.
scenarios.hint: Decay shrinks the old frame — but what is the shader adding to it each frame?
objectives: Stabilize feedback shaders with loop-gain analysis and soft clamping
evidence: Explain why a fixed decay cannot stabilize an additive feedback loop

scenarios.title: Shader Meets the Pipeline
scenarios.situation: Your installation needs the shader piece to react to the depth camera AND send its output to both the projector and a recording. Currently the camera analysis runs on the CPU, the shader on the GPU, and you copy the framebuffer back to the CPU for recording — the readback stalls the whole pipeline.
scenarios.prompt: How should you architect the data flow?
choices: Keep pixels on the GPU end to end: upload camera data as a texture once, do all analysis-driven visuals in shaders, and record via GPU-side capture (canvas.captureStream / MediaRecorder) instead of readPixels — the CPU never touches a pixel
Accept the stall — readback is unavoidable for recording
Move the shader computation to the CPU so everything is in one place
Record with an external camera pointed at the projection
scenarios.why: readPixels forces a GPU→CPU sync stall — the pipeline's worst bottleneck. The architecture principle is: cross the CPU/GPU boundary as rarely as possible. Camera → texture upload (one crossing), everything visual stays GPU-side, and captureStream records the composited output without ever pulling pixels back. The CPU handles only control logic and parameters.
scenarios.hint: Count the CPU↔GPU crossings in your current pipeline — which one can you delete entirely?
objectives: Architect GPU-resident pipelines that minimize readback
evidence: Name the API that records canvas output without readPixels

domains.name: Audio-Reactive Systems
domains.description: Make visuals listen: FFT analysis, beat detection, and mapping sound to motion.

scenarios.title: The Seizure Visual
scenarios.situation: Your audio-reactive piece looks amazing on your test track but jitters violently — clients call it 'uncomfortable'. The FFT values feed directly into scale and rotation.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
choices: Reduce the overall volume — quieter audio means calmer visuals

Add exponential smoothing per mapped parameter (lerp current toward target each frame, e.g., 0.85–0.95 factor), and consider attack/release asymmetry: fast attack for beats, slow release for decays. Raw FFT is noise; smoothing composes it into motion
Use a different audio file — the track is the problem
Lower the frame rate — fewer updates means less jitter
scenarios.why: Raw FFT bins jump wildly frame-to-frame; mapping them directly turns noise into motion sickness. Exponential smoothing (smoothed += (target - smoothed) * (1 - factor)) tames it while staying responsive. Attack/release asymmetry — react fast to onsets, decay slowly — mimics how humans perceive rhythm and looks intentional rather than nervous. This is compositional craft, not a volume knob.
scenarios.hint: Is the data noisy or is the mapping noisy? What turns jitter into groove?
evidence: Mapping
bass bin → scale (direct), highs → rotation (direct)
Feedback
'Uncomfortable', 'seizure-like' from 3 viewers.

scenarios.title: Mapping the Drop
scenarios.situation: You're building visuals for a DJ set. Mapping raw amplitude to particle size looks okay during loud sections but the visuals go dead during quiet breakdowns — then violently explode when the drop hits. The DJ says it feels 'disconnected' from the music.
scenarios.prompt: What mapping strategy keeps visuals alive across the full dynamic range of a set?
choices: Increase the amplitude multiplier so quiet sections are visible too

Split the spectrum into bands (bass/mids/highs) with per-band normalization and attack/release smoothing, and map musical features (bass energy → pulse, spectral centroid → hue, beat phase → motion) instead of raw amplitude → size
Map amplitude logarithmically — that alone fixes dynamic range
Ask the DJ to compress their mix so the dynamics are flatter
scenarios.why: Raw amplitude has 60dB+ of dynamic range; any linear map wastes most of it on the drop. Per-band normalization gives each frequency region its own full visual range, attack/release smoothing mimics how ears perceive onsets, and feature mapping (not amplitude mapping) connects visuals to musical structure — the drop reads as an event, not a volume spike.
scenarios.hint: What does the music have during a quiet breakdown that raw amplitude says is 'nothing'?
objectives: Map musical features (bands, onsets, spectral shape) instead of raw amplitude
evidence: Name three audio features more musical than raw amplitude

scenarios.title: Latency on Stage
scenarios.situation: At soundcheck, your visuals lag the kick drum by ~200ms — visibly off to the whole room. The chain: venue mixer → your laptop mic input → browser AnalyserNode → visuals. The FOH engineer offers you a direct feed from the mixer.
scenarios.prompt: What do you accept, and how do you kill the remaining latency?
choices: Take the direct line feed (kills room delay + mic processing), set analyser smoothing to minimum, read the analyser late in the frame, and consider onset prediction (trigger visuals on detected beat phase slightly early) since some OS audio latency is irreducible
Keep the mic — room sound is more 'alive' than a direct feed
Increase the FFT size for better bass resolution, which will tighten timing
Add a manual offset slider and eyeball it during the show
scenarios.why: The mic path adds room acoustics delay, OS mic processing, and ambient bleed; a direct feed removes all three at once — the single biggest win. Then minimize the reducible: smoothing smears transients, early-frame reads add a frame of lag. The irreducible OS buffer latency (~20-50ms) is handled by prediction: visuals fire on beat-phase anticipation, which also looks more musical than reaction.
scenarios.hint: Which single change removes the room, the mic processing, and the crowd noise from your signal path at once?
objectives: Minimize live audio latency: direct feed, minimal smoothing, prediction
evidence: List the latency sources in the mic path that a direct feed eliminates

scenarios.title: When the Audio Dies
scenarios.situation: Mid-performance, the venue's feed cuts out for 90 seconds. Your visuals freeze completely — the room watches a static image while the DJ keeps playing. Afterward the client calls it 'the dead minute and a half'.
scenarios.prompt: What fallback design prevents a dead show when the audio source fails?
choices: Show a 'SIGNAL LOST' message so the audience knows it's not your fault

Design an autonomous mode: when input energy stays below a threshold for N seconds, crossfade to a self-driving generative mode (seeded, tempo-estimated from recent history); crossfade back when signal returns — the show never stops, it just changes character
Freeze on the last good frame — at least it's a nice image
Keep a backup laptop with the same setup ready to swap in
scenarios.why: The audience doesn't care whose fault it is — they paid for a show. An autonomous fallback with tempo memory keeps the room alive; the crossfade (not a cut) hides the transition. 'SIGNAL LOST' announces failure; freezing admits defeat. Redundant hardware doesn't help when the venue's feed itself is the failure.
scenarios.hint: What should the audience experience during those 90 seconds — and does it require the venue's cable?
objectives: Design graceful audio-failure fallbacks with autonomous modes
evidence: Describe the trigger condition and transition for fallback mode

scenarios.title: The Festival Rig
scenarios.situation: You're booked for an outdoor festival: daylight stage, 4K LED wall, your laptop must drive it for 6 hours. Your studio piece runs fullscreen shaders at 60fps on your machine, but the LED processor adds its own scaling and the daylight washes out your dark aesthetic.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct performance and presentation setup?
choices: Rework for the rig: render at the wall's native resolution (not 4K unless the wall is), boost contrast/saturation for daylight (design a 'day mode' palette), cap frame rate to the wall's refresh, bring a redundant machine with the project synced, and test with the actual LED processor beforehand
Run the studio piece as-is; the LED wall will handle it
Turn up the laptop brightness to compensate for daylight
Ask the festival to run your piece after dark instead
scenarios.why: LED walls are not monitors: they have fixed native resolutions, their own scalers (which add latency and artifacts if you feed them wrong sizes), and daylight destroys low-contrast aesthetics. A day-mode palette is a design decision, not a brightness slider. Redundancy is non-negotiable for 6-hour outdoor runs — heat and dust kill laptops. Testing with the actual processor catches the scaler surprises.
scenarios.hint: What are the three ways an LED wall differs from your studio monitor — resolution, light, and what else?
objectives: Adapt audio-visual work for LED walls and daylight conditions
evidence: List the pre-show checks specific to an LED-wall deployment

scenarios.title: MIDI Mapping That Musicians Trust
scenarios.situation: A musician wants to control your visuals live from their MIDI controller during the set — filter sweeps mapped to visual intensity, pads triggering scene changes. Your first attempt maps CC values directly, and the visuals jitter with every tiny knob movement; scene changes sometimes double-trigger.
scenarios.prompt: How do you build MIDI control that feels professional?
choices: Map CC values directly but increase the visual response speed so jitter is less noticeable
Use only note-on messages and ignore continuous controllers entirely
Let the musician control the mouse instead — simpler

Add per-control slew limiting (smooth the CC stream), hysteresis/deadband on thresholds, require note-on velocity or a deliberate gesture for scene changes (with a 500ms lockout), and give the musician a small monitor showing current mapping state
scenarios.why: MIDI CCs are 7-bit (128 steps) and noisy — direct mapping turns quantization into visible jitter; slew limiting restores smoothness. Scene changes need deliberate-gesture semantics (velocity threshold + lockout) because an accidental double-trigger mid-set is a show-killer. The monitor closes the loop: the musician must see what the visuals think the controls are doing.
scenarios.hint: What is the bit depth of a MIDI CC, and what does that imply for direct 1:1 mapping?
objectives: Build robust MIDI mappings: smoothing, hysteresis, deliberate triggers
evidence: Explain why a scene-change trigger needs a lockout period

scenarios.title: Live Troubleshooting Protocol
scenarios.situation: Ten minutes before doors, your visuals show only a flat line on the audio input meter. The DJ is soundchecking, the cable is plugged in, and your code worked yesterday. Panic is setting in.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct 10-minute triage order?
choices: Follow the signal path in order: verify the source (is the mixer sending? check with headphones), verify the OS sees input (system sound settings / input meter), verify the browser has mic permission and the right device selected, then check your code's input node — fix at the first broken link, and have the autonomous fallback armed regardless
Restart everything: laptop, software, audio interface — in that order
Rewrite the audio input code — it must be a code bug since it worked yesterday
Ask the DJ to turn up their output until the meter moves
scenarios.why: Triage follows the signal: source → OS → browser → code. Each check takes 30 seconds and localizes the fault; random restarts waste the 10 minutes and may not touch the actual break (e.g., the browser silently switched to the laptop mic). 'Worked yesterday' points at environment, not code. Arming the fallback first means the show survives even if triage fails.
scenarios.hint: What changed between yesterday's working setup and today's venue — your code, or everything around it?
objectives: Triage live audio failures along the signal path under time pressure
evidence: State the four triage checkpoints in order

scenarios.title: Choosing the Audio Source
scenarios.situation: For a permanent museum installation, you must choose the audio input: a microphone in the room, a feed from the museum's ambient sound system, or fully synthesized audio with no external input. The piece should feel alive but run unattended for a year.
scenarios.prompt: Which source do you choose, and what does the choice imply for maintenance?
choices: Synthesized/internal audio: it is deterministic, needs no calibration, can't be unplugged or drowned by a school group, and has zero privacy concerns; use the room mic only as an optional modulation layer with a fallback to internal when it goes quiet — unattended longevity beats liveness
The microphone — real room sound is the most alive option
The museum's sound system feed — professional audio, no mic issues
No audio at all; make the piece purely time-based
scenarios.why: A year unattended is the real constraint: mics drift, get unplugged, pick up HVAC, and raise privacy questions in a museum. Internal synthesis is the only source with zero external dependencies — it cannot fail. The mic-as-modulation compromise keeps some liveness while the internal engine guarantees the piece never goes dead. External feeds add a dependency on another team's system.
scenarios.hint: What are the failure modes of each source over 365 unattended days?
objectives: Choose installation audio sources for unattended longevity
evidence: Name three failure modes of a room mic over a year

domains.name: From Screen to Installation
domains.description: Take generative work into physical space: projection, sensors, and the logistics of real installations.

scenarios.title: Hardware: PC vs Embedded
scenarios.situation: Your 3-month gallery installation needs to run a real-time particle system on a 4K projector. Option A: a gaming PC ($1,800) with full GPU power. Option B: a single-board computer ($150) running a simplified version. The gallery has no IT staff and the piece must survive unattended.
scenarios.prompt: How do you decide between the PC and the embedded board?
choices: Choose by constraint analysis: if the simplified version preserves the artistic intent, the board wins on reliability (no fans, no OS updates, boots to the piece), cost, and theft risk; choose the PC only if the full-fidelity version is the work — then budget for remote management, UPS, and a maintenance contract
Always choose the PC — more power is always better for art
Choose the cheaper option to maximize profit
Let the gallery decide — it's their space
scenarios.why: The decision is about unattended survival, not specs. A fanless board that boots straight into the piece and can't install updates is operationally superior for 3 months — fewer moving parts, literally and figuratively. The PC is justified only when fidelity IS the artwork, and then its true cost includes UPS, remote access, and someone on call. Price tags lie; total operational cost decides.
scenarios.hint: What kills unattended PCs in galleries — lack of GPU power, or something else entirely?
objectives: Select installation hardware by operational constraints
evidence: List the hidden operational costs of a gallery PC

scenarios.title: Budgeting the Real Cost
scenarios.situation: A venue offers $12,000 for a 2-month installation. Your hardware estimate is $4,000 and you figure 4 weeks of your time. It looks profitable — until you remember the last show's surprise costs.
scenarios.prompt: What budget structure prevents the last show's surprises?
choices: $4,000 hardware + 4 weeks labor = the budget; surprises are just bad luck

Build the full-cost budget: hardware + spares (10-15%), shipping both ways, insurance, your labor at day rate (build + install + deinstall + on-call), travel/lodging, contingency (15-20%), and teardown/disposal — then check the $12,000 against THAT total before signing
Double the hardware estimate and hope it covers everything
Ask for $20,000 without justification and negotiate down
scenarios.why: Installation economics die in the unbilled lines: return shipping of a projector rig, the spare sensor when one dies week 3, three on-call trips, deinstall labor nobody quoted. Spares + contingency aren't pessimism — they're the measured historical rate of 'surprises'. If the full-cost total exceeds $12,000, you negotiate scope or fee BEFORE signing, not after the money's gone.
scenarios.hint: What did the last show cost that wasn't in the original estimate — list them, then budget those lines first.
objectives: Build full-cost installation budgets with spares and contingency
evidence: Name five budget lines artists routinely forget

scenarios.title: Negotiating with the Venue
scenarios.situation: The venue contract makes you liable for 'any damage to the space' and requires you to carry insurance you don't have. They also want the piece running during their gala — outside your agreed hours — 'as a favor'.
scenarios.prompt: What do you negotiate before signing?
choices: Sign as-is — venues never enforce those clauses
Refuse to sign anything and work on a handshake

Negotiate liability to cover only negligence (not pre-existing conditions), get event insurance for the run (often $200-500, billable to the project), define operating hours explicitly with overtime rates, and put the gala in writing as paid extra hours — never accept open-ended liability or free extras verbally
Buy annual insurance immediately regardless of this show
scenarios.why: 'Any damage' without a condition report means you can inherit blame for existing wear — liability must be bounded and documented with pre-install photos. Event insurance per-show is cheap and standard; the venue often reimburses it. The gala 'favor' sets the precedent that your time is free — writing it as paid overtime protects every future ask. Verbal extras evaporate when invoices come.
scenarios.hint: Which clause could make you pay for damage you didn't cause — and what document prevents that?
objectives: Negotiate venue contracts: liability bounds, insurance, paid overtime
evidence: Name the document that bounds your liability for space damage

scenarios.title: Maintenance Planning
scenarios.situation: Your 6-month museum installation uses a depth camera, a PC, and a projector. The museum is 3 hours away. In month 2, the camera starts dropping frames; by month 3, dust has dimmed the projector noticeably.
scenarios.prompt: What maintenance plan should have been in the contract?
choices: A scheduled plan: remote monitoring (heartbeat + screenshots to your phone), a local contact trained on the 3 most common fixes (reboot sequence, cable reseat, lens clean), quarterly on-site visits billed in the contract, and a spares kit left on-site (camera, cables, filters) — with response-time tiers priced in
Hope nothing breaks — the hardware is new
Drive there whenever they call, billing hourly
Replace all hardware with industrial-rated versions and skip maintenance
scenarios.why: Distance turns every glitch into a crisis without a plan. Remote heartbeat monitoring catches the camera dropout before visitors notice; a trained local contact resolves 80% of issues in minutes; quarterly visits handle dust and drift proactively; on-site spares collapse a 3-hour-drive-plus-shipping repair into a swap. Response tiers (remote < 24h, on-site < 1 week) make expectations contractual, not emotional.
scenarios.hint: What breaks on a 6-month timeline — and which of those can someone already at the museum fix?
objectives: Design maintenance plans for long-run installations
evidence: List the contents of an on-site spares kit

scenarios.title: Power and Safety
scenarios.situation: Your outdoor night installation runs 12V LED strips (40A total), a projector, and a PC from a single venue outlet via daisy-chained extension cords. During testing, a cord feels warm. The venue asks for your 'safety plan'.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct power and safety approach?
choices: Do a proper load calculation (40A at 12V = 480W plus projector/PC — size the supply and wiring for 125% of continuous load), run dedicated circuits instead of daisy chains, use a licensed electrician for anything above low-voltage, add GFCI/RCD protection outdoors, secure all cables against trip hazards, and document it — warm cords are the warning before the fire
The warm cord is normal; wrap it in tape and proceed
Switch to battery power to avoid the venue's wiring entirely
Reduce brightness until the cord cools down
scenarios.why: Warm cords mean undersized conductors or overloaded circuits — the precursor to melted insulation. The 125% rule for continuous loads is electrical code, not caution; daisy-chained extensions multiply contact resistance at every joint. Outdoor + public + electricity demands GFCI protection and trip-proof cable runs. The 'safety plan' is also a legal document: if someone trips or worse, it proves due diligence.
scenarios.hint: What does a warm extension cord tell you about current vs conductor size?
objectives: Apply electrical safety fundamentals to installations
evidence: Compute the wattage of a 40A 12V LED run and state the sizing rule

scenarios.title: Teardown Planning
scenarios.situation: Your installation closes Sunday night. The venue needs the space clear by Monday 9 AM for the next show. Your piece involves a ceiling-mounted projector, 200m of cable clipped to walls, and custom steel frames. You've never planned a teardown.
scenarios.prompt: What does a professional teardown plan include?
choices: Show up Sunday night with a friend and figure it out
Hire movers Monday morning and let them handle it

A teardown plan built during INSTALL: labeled cables and a cable map, a reverse-order checklist (mounts last-on-first-off), booked labor for the actual hours (teardown takes ~50% of install time), venue sign-off on wall/ceiling restoration, packed transport with an inventory list, and a storage destination confirmed before closing night
Leave the mounting hardware — the venue can keep it
scenarios.why: Teardown is install in reverse, and it must be designed during install: unlabeled cables become a tangled loss, and ceiling mounts removed wrong damage the venue (your liability). The 50% rule budgets real hours — rushing causes the damage and injuries. Venue sign-off with photos closes the liability loop. No storage destination means hardware lives in your car for months.
scenarios.hint: When is the cheapest time to label a cable — during install, or at midnight during teardown?
objectives: Plan teardowns during install: labeling, checklists, sign-off
evidence: State the teardown time rule-of-thumb relative to install

scenarios.title: Sensor Placement in Public Space
scenarios.situation: Your interactive floor piece uses overhead depth cameras to track visitors. In testing, tracking fails when the room is crowded (occlusions), when someone wears black (absorption), and near the entrance where sunlight hits the floor.
scenarios.prompt: How do you make tracking robust in real public conditions?
choices: Buy more expensive cameras with better specs
Limit entry to 5 visitors at a time so tracking stays clean

Design for the hostile environment: mount cameras high and angled to reduce occlusion, define the active zone away from the sunlit entrance (or shade it), tune for dark clothing (raise exposure/gain for IR), add redundant overlapping coverage so one blocked camera doesn't kill tracking, and gracefully degrade (fewer tracked blobs, not a crash) when conditions are worst
Switch to pressure sensors in the floor instead
scenarios.why: Public space is adversarial: crowds occlude, black clothes absorb IR, sunlight blinds depth sensors. Robustness comes from geometry (height/angle beats specs), environmental control (shade the zone), sensor tuning for the worst case (dark clothing, not the average), redundancy (overlap), and graceful degradation. Crowd limits fight the venue's interests; sensor swaps restart the whole design.
scenarios.hint: Which failures are about the room, and which are about the sensor — and which can you fix with a ladder?
objectives: Harden sensor installations against real public-space conditions
evidence: Name three environmental mitigations that don't involve buying new sensors

scenarios.title: The Handoff Document
scenarios.situation: You're handing a 4-month installation to the venue's technician, who has never seen your system. It involves a PC that must boot into the piece, a projector with specific settings, and a sensor that needs weekly cleaning. Last time you did this verbally, the piece was down for a week.
scenarios.prompt: What does the handoff package contain?
choices: Your phone number — they can call with questions
The full source code and system passwords
A 2-hour training session, after which they're on their own

A runbook: one-page 'is it working?' check with photos of correct states, the exact boot/reboot sequence, projector settings with photos of the menus, the weekly cleaning procedure, a laminated 'if this, then that' troubleshooting card for the 5 most common failures, spare parts location, and escalation contacts with response times
scenarios.why: Verbal handoffs evaporate; the technician needs answers at 9 PM when you're unreachable. Photos of correct states let a non-expert verify at a glance; the exact boot sequence prevents the 'I rebooted it wrong' failure; the if-this-then-that card resolves the common cases without expertise; spares location + escalation tiers define what happens when the card runs out. Source code without a runbook is useless to a venue tech.
scenarios.hint: What does the technician need at 9 PM on a Saturday when the piece is dark and you're not answering?
objectives: Write venue handoff runbooks for non-expert technicians
evidence: List the five sections of an installation runbook

lessons.title: Canvas & Drawing — Core concepts
concepts: draw() loop: without background() at the top of draw(), each frame paints over the last — the 'trail' effect. Render the static stars once into an offscreen buffer (let pg = createGraphics(w, h)), then image(pg, 0, 0) each frame and draw only the 50 ships dynamically.
background(): calling background() clears the canvas every frame for clean animation.
rectMode: default rectMode(CORNER): the first two args are the top-left corner, and with y growing downward the rect extends right and down from (100, 100).
Coordinate system: the coordinate system (origin top-left, y down) is the source of half of all beginner layout bugs.

push()/pop(): wrap the blue rect in push()/pop() to sandbox its style, or set fill() again before the third shape. push()/pop() save and restore both styles and transformations; forgetting pop() is the classic state-leak.
Drawing state: fill() sets persistent drawing state — everything after fill(0,0,255) stays blue until changed.

example.walkthrough: Hue 180° on the color wheel is cyan, at 80% saturation and 90% brightness. HSB separates 'which color' (hue) from 'how intense' (saturation) and 'how bright' — which is why generative artists love it: sweep the hue for rainbows, fix saturation/brightness for harmony. Forgetting colorMode is active is a classic source of 'wrong color' bugs.

pitfalls: Common trap: use createGraphics() for an offscreen buffer: compose the static layer once, then image() it each frame.
Common trap: HSB mode doesn't change fill().
Common trap: the canvas can't change size after setup.
Common trap: use fixed pixel positions everywhere.

lessons.title: Animation — Core concepts
concepts: frameCount: x = (frameCount * 2) % width: frameCount is a free frame clock, and modulo wraps it.
Motion basics: (For perfect GIF loops, make sure the motion period divides the frame count.). Fixed per-frame increments are the simplest motion; the modulo makes it loop.

noise(): noise(t) returns smooth Perlin noise — nearby inputs give nearby outputs, so advancing t slowly yields wandering, organic paths. random() jumps discontinuously every call; sin() is too regular. noise() with slowly-advancing offsets (optionally separate offsets per axis) is the signature move of generative motion.

Organic motion: this exponential ease-out is the most-used motion feel in creative coding (and UI animation). Frame-counted motion ties your artwork's timing to the viewer's hardware — deltaTime decouples them.
lerp(): lerp(x, target, 0.05) moves 5% of the remaining distance per frame — fast at first, then asymptotically settling.

example.code:
let x, y, vx, vy;
// ball should bounce around the canvas forever
example.walkthrough: When the ball's edge crosses a wall, flip the perpendicular velocity component (vx *= -1 for side walls). Account for the radius (x > width - r) so it bounces visually at the edge, not past it. Velocity + boundary reflection is the seed of every physics sketch — gravity, friction, and springs all layer onto this pattern.

pitfalls: Common trap: move x by a fixed 5 pixels per frame toward the target.
Common trap: cap the frame rate with frameRate(30) and hope.
Common trap: random() each frame: jumpy and discontinuous.
Common trap: set x directly to the target; snapping is fine.

lessons.title: Generative Systems — Core concepts
concepts: RandomSeed(s) makes the pseudorandom sequence deterministic — same seed, same artwork, every time.
Controlled variation: smooth noise gives coherent variation — neighbors relate, nothing repeats mechanically, nothing dissolves into chaos.
Recursion expresses self-similarity directly: each branch is a smaller tree.

The seed becomes the edition number: share it and anyone can re-render the identical piece. This is how generative art platforms (Art Blocks-style) work: the token's seed IS the artwork's DNA.

pitfalls: Common trap: render at high resolution with pixelDensity() / large offscreen buffers, using fixed seeds so the export matches the preview.
Common trap: one particle is enough; systems don't scale.
Common trap: set randomSeed() / noiseSeed() before generating; same seed replays the piece exactly.

lessons.title: Interaction — Core concepts
concepts: map(): map(mouseX, 0, width, 0, 360) translates the mouse range into hue degrees — left edge red, right edge back to red. map() is the universal adapter between input ranges and visual ranges.

Mouse input: implement touchStarted()/touchMoved() alongside (or instead of) mouse handlers, and return false to stop the browser scrolling/zooming over your canvas. mousePressed sometimes fires on mobile, but unreliably — dedicated touch handlers are the robust path.
Event functions: mousePressed() is an event: it fires once per click. mouseIsPressed is state: true for every frame the button stays down (dozens of frames per click).

Polling vs events: events for discrete actions (spawn, toggle), polling for continuous ones (dragging, holding). A mode variable with a switch in draw() — each case self-contained, transitions triggered by events or timers.
KeyPressed() with (key === ' ') toggles pause once per press — discrete.
keyCode: note key holds the character, keyCode the physical key (arrows, shift) — use keyCode for arrows.

example.code: // artist wants to perform the piece live, tuning 3 parameters
example.walkthrough: let hueSlider = createSlider(0, 360, 180); then hue = hueSlider.value() in draw(). Sliders turn parameters into instruments — the piece becomes performable, and tuning becomes play instead of edit-compile cycles. Expose the 3–5 parameters that matter; hide the rest.

pitfalls: Common trap: createSlider() for live parameters: bind hue, speed, and complexity to sliders and read .value() in draw().
Common trap: use keyPressed() for discrete actions and check key / keyCode for which key; poll in draw() only for held-key movement.
Common trap: a state variable (e.g., mode = 'attract' | 'play' | 'rest') with a switch in draw() and transitions on events/timeout.
Common trap: map it: let hue = map(mouseX, 0, width, 0, 360);.

lessons.title: Math for Art — Core concepts
concepts: map(): map(sensor, 0, 1023, 20, 400) linearly translates ranges — the single most-used function in interactive art.
Polar coordinates (angle, radius) are the natural language of circular layouts — orbits, radial menus, flower petals, clock faces.
Radians: fix with rotate(radians(45)) or angleMode(DEGREES) in setup().
lerpColor: loop over rows: t = y / height; stroke(lerpColor(blue, orange, t)); line across. lerpColor interpolates every channel by t — the color twin of lerp().
dist(): if (dist(a.x, a.y, b.x, b.y) < 60) line(...). dist() is Euclidean distance in one call — the basis of connection effects, repulsion, attraction, and collision.

example.code: // want: 12 dots evenly spaced on a circle of radius 150
example.walkthrough: For i in 0..11: a = i * TWO_PI / 12; x = cx + 150*cos(a); y = cy + 150*sin(a). TWO_PI/12 spaces them evenly; cos/sin project onto x/y.

pitfalls: Common trap: use the golden angle 137.5°: each seed at angle i*137.5°, radius growing with sqrt(i).
Common trap: check every pair with nested ifs on raw coordinates.
Common trap: map(sensor, 0, 1023, 20, 400): translate the 10-bit range into a radius range.
Common trap: rotate() takes degrees; the code is fine.

lessons.title: Showcase — Core concepts
concepts: Performance: creative-coding performance is almost always about doing less per frame, not faster hardware. Present like a projectionist, not a programmer: the piece is the performance.
Responsive generative art is layout-as-function.
prefers-reduced-motion: check matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)') and offer a calm alternative: static composition, slow drift, no flashing.

example.code: 3000 particles with shadows and blur: 9 fps. Target: 60.
example.walkthrough: Kill the expensive per-frame ops first: shadows/blur are brutally costly — fake them with gradients or drop them. Then: fewer objects, noStroke(), no per-frame allocations (GC pauses), static layers into buffers.

pitfalls: Common trap: add a prefers-reduced-motion check: offer a static or gentle mode when the user requests reduced motion.
Common trap: fullscreen presentation: fullscreen(true) on interaction, noCursor(), hide UI chrome.
Common trap: motion is the art; accessibility doesn't apply.
Common trap: read the code aloud as the presentation.

lessons.title: Creative Coding — Core concepts
concepts: The canvas is a bitmap with two sizes: the backing store (actual pixels) and the CSS box (logical pixels). Multiply the backing store by devicePixelRatio and scale the context, or high-DPI screens turn your art to mush.

Animate with requestAnimationFrame, not timers: it syncs to vsync, sleeps in background tabs, and hands you a timestamp — use the delta so motion speed is frame-rate independent across 60 Hz and 120 Hz displays.

Generative art is deterministic randomness: a seeded PRNG (like mulberry32) turns the seed into the artwork's identity — same seed, same piece, re-renderable at any size, shareable as a single number.

WebGL splits work by frequency: the vertex shader runs per vertex (geometry, transforms), the fragment shader runs per pixel (color, detail). High-frequency detail like noise belongs in the fragment stage.
Trails and feedback effects are exponential decay, not accumulation: fade the frame with a translucent background rect each tick instead of adding light forever, or the image clips to white.
GLSL precision is a portability concern: declare precision explicitly, request highp where noise/math needs it, and provide mediump fallbacks — mobile GPUs do not guarantee desktop defaults.

example.walkthrough: mulberry32 is a tiny, well-known seeded generator. Every call advances a deterministic sequence, so the entire composition derives from the initial seed — the prized output can be re-rendered exactly by reusing its seed.

pitfalls: Common trap: setting canvas.width/height via CSS only — the backing store stays 300×150 default and everything stretches blurry.
Common trap: assuming 16 ms per frame — on 120 Hz displays or throttled tabs your motion runs at the wrong speed; always use the rAF timestamp delta.
Common trap: Math.random() everywhere — the artwork can never be reproduced, versioned, or re-rendered at print resolution; seed your randomness.
Common trap: computing per-pixel detail in the vertex shader — 4 vertices cannot carry a noise field; that work belongs in the fragment shader.
