lessons.title: Portfolio Review Exam Strategy
concepts: Portfolio Review tests applied judgment more than memorization. Roughly a third of questions are scenario-based: read the situation, eliminate distractors, pick the BEST answer — not merely a correct one.
Performance-based questions (PBQs) simulate real tasks: drag-and-drop, CLI output analysis, log reading. The labs in this bootcamp are PBQ rehearsal — treat every lab as exam practice.
Time budget: divide total minutes by question count before you start, then check the clock every 20 questions. Flag hard questions and move on — a stuck minute is a lost minute.
Elimination first: cross out the two obviously wrong choices, then compare the remaining two against the question's constraints (cheapest? most secure? first step?).
Never leave a question blank. There is no penalty for wrong answers — an educated guess beats an empty one every time.

example.code:
Q: 'A user reports... Which should you do FIRST?'
  → The word FIRST is the whole question.
  → Eliminate any choice that is a later step.
  → Among the rest, pick the diagnostic before the fix.
example.walkthrough: Exam writers love FIRST, BEST, MOST, and LEAST. Those words change the answer even when the scenario looks identical. Read the actual question stem twice — once for the story, once for the ask.

pitfalls: Answering the scenario instead of the question — the story is context; the final sentence is the task.
Changing answers on review without new evidence — first instincts outperform second-guessing statistically.
Memorizing acronyms without understanding the process behind them — PBQs punish surface knowledge.
lessons.try_it: Take any scenario in this bootcamp, cover the choices, and write what the question is really asking in one sentence before looking at options.

lessons.title: Study System: Spaced Repetition That Sticks
concepts: Forgetting is the default — plan for it. Review a domain's key concepts at expanding intervals: 1 day, 3 days, 7 days, 14 days. Each successful recall strengthens the memory trace.
Active recall beats re-reading: close the lesson and explain the concept aloud in your own words. If you cannot explain it, you do not know it yet.
Interleave domains instead of block-studying one: mix scenarios from two domains in a session. Exams mix topics — your practice should too.
The Feynman check: after each lesson, write a 3-sentence explanation a junior could follow. Vague sentences reveal vague understanding.
Weekly rhythm: 2 domains + one finished sketch per week; portfolio curation at week 4 and 6.

example.code:
Session template (90 min):
  0-10   warm-up: 5 flashcards / quick recalls
  10-50  new domain: lessons + knowledge checks
  50-75  scenarios from today + one older domain (interleaving)
  75-90  one terminal lab, then 3-sentence Feynman writes
example.walkthrough: Ninety focused minutes beat four distracted hours. The template above is engineered for retention, not seat time — protect the lab block, it is where skills become reflexes.

pitfalls: Re-reading notes and calling it studying — recognition is not recall; the exam tests recall.
Cramming new domains the night before — sleep consolidates memory; an all-nighter trades retention for exhaustion.
Skipping the Feynman write — it feels slow, but it is the fastest diagnostic of real understanding.
lessons.try_it: Do one Feynman write right now: explain in 3 sentences what a bootcamp 'domain' is and why the order matters.

lessons.title: Systems Thinking: Your Unfair Advantage
concepts: Exams and interviews reward systems thinkers: people who trace a request end-to-end instead of reciting isolated facts. This bootcamp trains that explicitly in the Systems Anatomy domain.
The four-step method: (1) see the whole in context, (2) cut it open to reveal layers, (3) walk the process step-by-step, (4) pull apart into labeled pieces.
Every troubleshooting scenario here is a systems trace in disguise: start from the symptom, walk backward through dependencies, find where the expected flow diverges from reality.
In interviews, narrate the journey: 'the request starts here, then…' — hiring managers hear senior-level thinking when you trace instead of define.
The Systems Anatomy explorer in Visuals lets you step through living systems click by click. Use it before each domain's scenarios.

example.code:
Weak answer: 'DNS resolves names to IPs.'
Strong answer: 'The stub resolver asks the recursive resolver, which walks root → TLD → authoritative, caching at each level — that is why the first lookup is slow and the second is instant.'
example.walkthrough: One narrated journey demonstrates more competence than ten memorized definitions. Practice this voice in every scenario's 'why' explanation — read them aloud.

pitfalls: Defining terms instead of tracing flows when asked 'how does X work?'
Jumping to fixes before mapping the system — fixes applied to the wrong layer waste time and credibility.
Treating each domain as separate — the mock assessment deliberately chains them; practice connecting domains now.
lessons.try_it: Open the Systems Anatomy domain and step through one full system in the explorer before your first study session.

lessons.title: Mock Assessment Briefing: Rules of Engagement
concepts: The mock simulates Portfolio Review conditions: timed, mixed-domain, no hints, one shot per question. Treat it as the real exam — same chair, same focus, no phone.
Scoring mirrors the real exam's weighting: scenario judgment counts more than recall. A wrong answer on a multi-step scenario costs more than a missed definition.
Run the mock only after all domains show 80%+ mastery. Running it early wastes its diagnostic value — it is a measuring instrument, not a study tool.
After each run, the review breaks down misses by domain. Your next study block targets exactly those domains — the mock tells you where to aim.
Two full runs minimum: the first finds gaps, the second confirms they are closed. A passing second run is your green light.

example.code:
Mock protocol:
  1. Silence notifications, full-screen the bootcamp
  2. Note start time; budget per-question time on paper
  3. Answer every question — no blanks
  4. Flag-and-move on stuck questions; return with fresh eyes
  5. Review the domain breakdown before any celebration
example.walkthrough: The mock's value is the breakdown, not the score. A 68% with a clear miss-map beats a lucky 82% — the map tells you exactly what to study next.

pitfalls: Peeking at notes mid-mock — it inflates the score and destroys the diagnostic.
Running the mock as a first activity — without domain mastery it only measures unpreparedness.
Ignoring the domain breakdown — the score is trivia; the miss-map is the study plan.
lessons.try_it: Check your domain mastery percentages now. List any domain under 80% — those are your pre-mock targets.

lessons.title: Reviewing a Mock Run: Turning Misses into Mastery
concepts: For every missed question, classify the error: knowledge gap (never learned it), application gap (knew it, misapplied it), or reading error (misread the ask). Each type needs a different fix.
Knowledge gaps go back to the domain lesson — re-read, re-verify, Feynman-write. Application gaps need more scenarios, not more reading. Reading errors need the exam-strategy lesson again.
Keep an error log: question topic, error type, correct reasoning in one sentence. Patterns emerge fast — three 'reading errors' in a row is a process problem, not a knowledge problem.
Re-test missed topics within 48 hours with fresh scenarios. A corrected mistake that is not re-tested is a mistake waiting to recur.
Your second mock run should show misses migrating: fewer knowledge gaps, zero repeated reading errors. That migration is the signal you are ready.

example.code:
Error log entry:
  Q: firewall rule order scenario → chose 'deny' before 'allow'
  Type: application gap (knew rule order, misapplied under time pressure)
  Fix: 5 more firewall scenarios, timed
  Correct reasoning: 'First match wins — the allow had to precede the deny.'
example.walkthrough: Do not just re-read the explanation and move on. The error log forces you to name the failure mode — and named failures are fixable failures.

pitfalls: Re-reading explanations passively — recognition feels like learning but evaporates under pressure.
Studying only the missed topics and neglecting maintenance review of strong ones — strengths decay too.
Taking the second mock too soon — give fixes 48 hours and a re-test cycle first.
lessons.try_it: Create your error log file now (paper or notes app). You will need it after your first mock run.

lessons.title: Capstone Plan: What You Will Build and Why
concepts: Employers and examiners trust demonstrated skill over claimed knowledge. Your capstone is a working artifact — something you can screenshare and narrate in under 10 minutes.
Pick ONE project from the list below. Depth beats breadth: a single polished build outperforms three half-finished ones.
Scope it to finish in 2–3 focused sessions. If it needs more, cut features — a complete small project beats an ambitious pile of parts.
Document as you go: every decision gets a one-line reason. That log becomes your interview narration script.
Done means: it works end-to-end, you can demo it live, and you can explain every part without notes.

example.code:
Pick your project:
  1. Interactive Installation Piece — a complete interactive work with documentation
  2. Generative Series — a coherent 12-piece series with process documentation
  3. Audio-Reactive Performance — a live audio-visual set with mapping documentation
example.walkthrough: Choose the project that scares you slightly — that is where the growth is. But cap the scope ruthlessly: you must finish.

pitfalls: Starting two projects and finishing neither — pick one, finish it, then consider a second.
Building without documenting — the demo narration is half the value; no log means no story.
Gold-plating instead of finishing — ship the working core first, polish only if time remains.
lessons.try_it: Write your one-paragraph project selection rationale now: which project, why it fits your goals, and what 'done' looks like.

lessons.title: Build Log: Decisions, Dead Ends, and Proof
concepts: Keep a build log with timestamps: what you tried, what happened, what you changed. Dead ends are valuable — they prove you debugged, not just followed a tutorial.
For each component, record: purpose (one line), how it works (three lines), how you tested it (one command or check).
Screenshot or record key milestones. A 60-second screen recording of the working project is worth more than a page of description.
Version your work: even a simple dated folder structure beats a single 'final' file. Show the progression.
The log is not overhead — it IS the deliverable's companion. Interviewers ask 'tell me about a challenge'; your log hands you the answer.

example.code:
Build log entry:
  14:32 — Tried X config; service failed with error Y
  14:47 — Found cause: Z was misconfigured (docs said A, reality was B)
  15:05 — Fixed; verified with [test command]; works end-to-end
example.walkthrough: Write the log as you go, not after. Memory lies; timestamps do not. Future-you (in the interview) will thank present-you.

pitfalls: Writing the log from memory at the end — you will forget the dead ends, which are the best stories.
Skipping the 'how I tested it' line — untested claims collapse under the first interview question.
No recordings — a live demo can fail; a recording is bulletproof backup.
lessons.try_it: Create your build log file now with today's date and your project title as the header.

lessons.title: Demo Day: Narrating Your Build in 10 Minutes
concepts: Structure the demo: problem (1 min) → architecture (2 min) → live walkthrough (5 min) → lessons learned (2 min). Rehearse it twice, timed.
Narrate the systems journey: 'a request starts here, flows through…' — the Systems Anatomy voice. Show you understand the whole, not just the parts you typed.
Prepare for three hard questions: 'why this approach over X?', 'what breaks at scale?', 'what would you do differently?'. Write your answers in advance.
Lead with the working demo, not slides. Working software presented live beats any deck.
End with the repo/README link and offer to walk through the code. Make it effortless for them to verify your work.

example.code:
Demo script skeleton:
  'I built [X] because [problem]. It works by [3-step journey].
   Watch: [live action]. The tricky part was [challenge] —
   I solved it by [approach]. Code and docs are at [link].'
example.walkthrough: Rehearsal is non-negotiable. A polished 10-minute demo signals preparation, communication skill, and genuine ownership — exactly what hiring managers screen for.

pitfalls: Wing the demo — 'let me just show you' without a plan wastes the moment.
Hiding the challenges — the dead ends and fixes are what prove real engineering happened.
No backup plan — have the recording ready in case live demo gods are unkind.
lessons.try_it: Draft your three hard-question answers now, before you build. They will sharpen your design decisions.

lessons.title: Roles That Hire Creative Coding Skills
concepts: The roles: Creative Technologist, New Media Artist, Interaction Designer, Technical Artist. Read 10 job postings and extract the repeated requirements — that list is your real syllabus.
Titles vary by company; skills cluster by function. Map postings to skill clusters (not titles) to see what the market actually buys.
Entry points differ: some roles hire on certification + projects, others on portfolio + interviews. Know your target's gate before optimizing for it.
Salary bands follow scarcity + impact: specialized + revenue-adjacent pays more. Position yourself at that intersection deliberately.
Track the market quarterly: which skills are rising in postings? Your learning backlog should follow the demand signal.

example.code:
Posting analysis template:
  Role: ___
  Repeated requirements (3+ postings): ___
  Nice-to-haves: ___
  My gaps: ___ → study priority
example.walkthrough: The job posting is the employer's requirements doc. Analyze it like one — systematically, not hopefully.

pitfalls: Chasing titles instead of skill clusters — the same skills hide under five different titles.
Ignoring the 'repeated requirements' — what 8/10 postings demand is the real bar.
No gap analysis — studying without knowing your gaps is motion without direction.
lessons.try_it: Pull 5 postings for your target role now. List the top 5 repeated requirements.

lessons.title: Resume & Projects That Get Callbacks
concepts: Resumes get 30 seconds: lead with a skills line matching the posting's keywords, then 3-4 bullets per role with quantified outcomes (not duties).
Projects beat buzzwords: one deployed, documented project outweighs a paragraph of claimed skills. Link the repo AND the live demo.
Tailor per application: mirror the posting's language for the top 5 requirements. ATS filters are literal — 'PostgreSQL' does not match 'postgres' in dumb parsers.
The capstone in this bootcamp IS your resume project: finish it, document it, link it. That single line does more work than any certification bullet.
GitHub profile hygiene: pinned repos with READMEs, green contribution squares, no empty forks. Recruiters do click through.

example.code:
Bullet formula: [Action verb] + [what] + [scale] + [outcome]
  Weak: 'Responsible for databases.'
  Strong: 'Migrated 2TB analytics DB to Postgres; cut query p95 40%; zero-downtime cutover.'
example.walkthrough: Every bullet must answer: what did you do, at what scale, to what effect? Duties describe jobs; outcomes get interviews.

pitfalls: Skill lists without evidence — every claimed skill needs a project or role bullet backing it.
One generic resume for all applications — tailoring is the highest-ROI 20 minutes in job hunting.
No links — a project without a URL might as well not exist.
lessons.try_it: Rewrite your weakest resume bullet using the formula above. Quantify something.

lessons.title: Interview Loops: What Actually Happens
concepts: Typical loop: recruiter screen (15 min, fit + comp) → technical screen (45-60 min, live problems) → onsite/virtual loop (3-5 rounds: technical depth, system design, behavioral) → offer.
Technical screens test thinking aloud: narrate your approach before coding/querying. Silence is scored as stuck; structured thinking is scored as senior.
Behavioral rounds use STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) — prepare 5 stories covering: conflict, failure, leadership, ambiguity, and impact. Quantify results.
Questions YOU ask matter: 'what does success look like in 90 days?' and 'what's the hardest problem the team faces?' signal seriousness. Never ask nothing.
Follow up within 24 hours: thank-you note referencing something specific from the conversation. Small effort, real signal.

example.code:
STAR story skeleton:
  S: 'Our deploy pipeline broke weekly...'
  T: 'I owned stabilizing it in Q3...'
  A: 'I added staged rollouts + runbook...'
  R: 'Deploys went from 60% to 99% success; on-call pages dropped 70%.'
example.walkthrough: Prepare stories, not scripts: know your 5 STAR stories cold enough to adapt to any behavioral question. Rehearse aloud twice.

pitfalls: No questions for them — reads as disinterest; always ask two.
Rambling technical answers — structure: approach first, then detail, then verify.
Badmouthing past employers — the interviewer hears how you will talk about THEM.
lessons.try_it: Draft one STAR story now using the skeleton. Time it — aim for 90 seconds.

lessons.title: The Creative Coding Tool Landscape
concepts: Tools cluster by job-to-be-done, not by vendor. Learn the categories first, then pick one tool per category deeply — depth in one beats surface in five.
The 80/20 rule: 20% of each tool's features cover 80% of real work. Master the core workflow before exploring the edges.
Free/open tiers are enough to learn: every major platform has a free tier or community edition sufficient for portfolio projects. Never pay to learn the basics.
Tool churn is constant; fundamentals are stable. SQL outlives every BI tool; TCP/IP outlives every cloud console. Invest in fundamentals first.

For Creative Coding, the essential categories:
  Framework: p5.js/openFrameworks
  Shaders: GLSL/Shadertoy
  Audio: Tone.js/Max
  Hardware: Arduino/Raspberry Pi

example.code:
Learning order:
  1. One tool per category, core workflow only
  2. Build the capstone using exactly these tools
  3. Add a second tool per category only when a job posting demands it
example.walkthrough: Resist tool tourism: each new tool costs weeks. The portfolio proves depth; the resume lists breadth honestly.

pitfalls: Learning 5 tools shallowly instead of 2 deeply — interviews probe depth.
Paying for premium tiers to learn — free tiers cover 90% of learning needs.
Chasing every new release — fundamentals first; novelty second.
lessons.try_it: List your one-tool-per-category stack now. Identify any category where you have zero depth — that is your next lab.

lessons.title: Workflows: Connecting the Tools
concepts: Tools in isolation are trivia; workflows are skill. The professional unit is the end-to-end flow: ingest → transform → validate → deliver — across YOUR tool stack.
Document your workflows as runbooks: trigger, steps, verification, rollback. A runbook turns personal knowledge into team capability.
Automate the toil, not the judgment: repetitive steps get scripted; decisions stay human. If you do it weekly, automate it.
Version everything: code, configs, queries, dashboards. 'Final_v2_ACTUAL' is not version control — git is.
The workflow IS the portfolio piece: 'here is my pipeline, here is the runbook, here is the monitoring' — that sentence hires.

example.code:
Runbook skeleton:
  Trigger: ___ (schedule/event/manual)
  Steps: 1.___ 2.___ 3.___
  Verify: ___ (how do you know it worked?)
  Rollback: ___ (how do you undo it?)
  Owner: ___  Last tested: ___
example.walkthrough: Write the runbook BEFORE automating: it forces you to understand the workflow well enough to hand it to someone else.

pitfalls: Automating before documenting — you encode confusion at machine speed.
No verification step — a workflow without a check is a hope with extra steps.
No rollback plan — the first failure without one teaches this lesson permanently.
lessons.try_it: Write a runbook for one workflow you do regularly, using the skeleton above.

lessons.title: Curating the Portfolio That Hires
concepts: Curate ruthlessly: 8–12 pieces, each earning its place. One weak piece drags down ten strong ones — kill your darlings.
Every piece needs the triad: the visual (hero image/video), the process (2-3 work-in-progress shots), the code link. Process shots prove the work is yours and show how you think.
Write the one-paragraph story per piece: what it explores, what technique, what surprised you. 'Pretty thing I made' is not a story; the inquiry is.
Video > images for time-based work: a 15-second loop shows motion that stills cannot. Host on the portfolio directly — dead external links kill credibility.
Order for impact: strongest first, strongest last, good in the middle. The first piece decides whether they scroll; the last decides what they remember.

example.code:
Piece page structure:
  Hero: 15s looping video, fullscreen-capable
  Story: 'An exploration of flow fields as weather systems —
    40k particles advected through curl noise, colored by velocity.'
  Process: 3 WIP frames (early ugly → tuned → final)
  Code: repo link + 'runs with: open index.html'
example.walkthrough: Hiring managers spend 60 seconds on a portfolio. The curation IS the skill being evaluated — taste, judgment, and the ability to finish.

pitfalls: 20+ pieces with no curation — volume signals you cannot judge your own work.
No process documentation — finished pieces without WIP read as possibly not-yours.
Broken demos and dead links — each one is a vote against your reliability.
lessons.try_it: Rank your current pieces 1-10. Cut everything below 7. Write the one-paragraph story for your top 3.

lessons.title: Your First Shader: Thinking in Parallel
concepts: A fragment shader runs once per pixel, all pixels in parallel. There is no 'previous pixel' — only position, time, and math. That constraint IS the aesthetic.
Start with the holy trinity: uv coordinates (where am I), time (uniform float), and noise (value noise → fbm). 80% of shader art is these three composed.
GLSL is C-like but parallel: no dynamic arrays, loops need constant bounds, precision matters on mobile. Write small, test often — shader errors are silent black screens.
fbm (fractal Brownian motion): layer noise at doubling frequencies, halving amplitudes, 4-5 octaves. It makes clouds, marble, terrain, fire — the organic texture primitive.
Prototype on Shadertoy, then port: the workflow is sketch-in-browser, refine, then integrate into your piece. Shadertoy is the sketchbook; your project is the canvas.

example.walkthrough: The shader mindset: stop thinking in objects and start thinking in fields — every pixel asks 'what am I?' and the math answers. That inversion unlocks the medium.

pitfalls: Treating shaders like CPU code — no shared state between pixels; embrace the constraint.
Skipping fbm — raw noise looks harsh; octaves make it organic. Learn fbm before anything fancy.
No precision qualifiers on mobile — works on desktop, breaks on phones; set them from the start.
lessons.try_it: Write the 10-line cloud shader above in a Shadertoy tab. Change the palette and speed — feel the trinity.

lessons.title: Making Visuals Listen: FFT Basics
concepts: FFT turns audio into frequency bins: bass lives low (~20-250Hz), mids carry melody, highs carry sparkle. Map bins to visual parameters deliberately — bass to scale, mids to color, highs to particle jitter.
Smoothing is everything: raw FFT data is jittery. Apply exponential smoothing (lerp toward target each frame) — responsive but not seizure-inducing.
Beat detection: track energy in the bass bins; a beat is a sharp rise above the rolling average. Use beats as triggers (spawn, flash, cut) — the audience FEELS the sync.
Design the mapping before coding: which frequencies drive which visuals, at what sensitivity. Random mapping looks random; composed mapping looks choreographed.
Test with varied music: your mapping must survive ambient AND techno. If it only works on one track, it is a demo, not a system.

example.code:
Mapping plan:
  bass (20-250Hz) → core scale (smoothed 0.85) + beat trigger
  mids (250-2kHz) → hue rotation (smoothed 0.9)
  highs (2k-20kHz) → particle emission rate
  beat → camera impulse + flash decay
example.walkthrough: Audio-reactive work is composition, not just code: the mapping plan is the score, the FFT is the instrument. Write the score first.

pitfalls: No smoothing — raw FFT jitter looks broken, not energetic.
Mapping everything to everything — visual noise; pick 3 mappings and commit.
Only testing one track — robustness across genres is the difference between demo and piece.
lessons.try_it: Write a mapping plan (like above) for a piece you imagine. Define bins, targets, and smoothing per mapping.

lessons.title: Installation Logistics: The Unsexy 80%
concepts: The work is 20% of an installation; logistics is 80%: power, mounting, ambient light, viewing distance, uptime, and the 'what if it crashes at 2 AM' plan.
Power budget first: count every device's draw, add 30% headroom, and know the venue's circuits. A tripped breaker during opening night is the classic failure.
Design for unattended operation: auto-start on boot, watchdog restarts, remote access for fixes. If it needs you babysitting, it is not installation-ready.
Light is the material: projection needs darkness, LEDs need diffusion, screens need viewing angles. Visit the space at the actual show time — noon light lies about evening conditions.
Document the install like a handover: one-page setup sheet, cable map, passwords, and the 'if X then Y' troubleshooting card. The venue tech will thank you at midnight.

example.code:
Install checklist:
  [ ] Power: total draw __W, circuits __, 30% headroom confirmed
  [ ] Boot: auto-start script tested with 3 cold boots
  [ ] Watchdog: restarts app on crash (tested by kill -9)
  [ ] Remote: SSH/VNC access verified from outside venue network
  [ ] Light: visited at show time, brightness adequate
  [ ] Handover: 1-page sheet + cable map printed
example.walkthrough: Installations are judged on uptime, not just beauty. The piece that runs flawlessly for 30 days beats the prettier one that crashed on day two.

pitfalls: No auto-start testing — 'it worked on my laptop' is not an installation plan.
Ignoring ambient light — the #1 aesthetic killer; scout at show time.
No remote access — every installation needs midnight fixes; plan the path in.
lessons.try_it: Write the install checklist for a hypothetical piece in a space you know. Identify the top 3 risks.

lessons.title: Pricing and Client Work
concepts: Pricing models: day rate (simple, common), project rate (scope-defined), licensing (for reusable work). Never hourly for creative — it punishes efficiency.
Scope in writing: deliverables, revisions (2-3 included), timeline, kill fee (50% if cancelled). The contract prevents the 'just one more change' death spiral.
Day rates anchor on value + market: research local rates, then price on the value delivered (an installation driving foot traffic is worth more than hours). Raise annually.
The 50/50 payment split: 50% upfront (non-refundable), 50% on delivery. No work without the deposit — this rule has saved more artists than any technique.
Say no to spec work and 'exposure': portfolio pieces you choose beat free client work. Exposure doesn't pay rent; curation does.

example.code:
Project quote:
  Interactive lobby piece: $8,000 project rate
  Includes: concept, build, install support, 2 revision rounds
  Terms: 50% deposit, 50% on acceptance; kill fee 50%
  Timeline: 6 weeks. Overage: $1,200/day.
  Written, signed, then work begins.
example.walkthrough: Business skills ARE creative skills: the artists who thrive treat contracts, pricing, and scope as part of the craft. Learn them deliberately.

pitfalls: Hourly billing for creative — punishes your speed; price the value.
No written scope — 'just one more tweak' becomes 40 unpaid hours.
Starting without deposit — the deposit is the client's commitment device.
lessons.try_it: Write a project quote for hypothetical work using the template. What would you charge per day? Research one data point.

lessons.title: Post-Processing Effects
concepts: Post-processing = fullscreen shader passes over the rendered scene: bloom, vignette, grain, chromatic aberration. The 'cinematic' look is mostly post.
Bloom: bright-pass (threshold) + blur (multi-scale) + add back. Glow without the GPU melting — the classic.
Vignette + grain: darken edges (focus), add animated grain (film feel). Two cheap effects that add enormous production value.
Chromatic aberration: offset RGB channels radially. Subtle = cinematic; strong = broken-lens aesthetic. A little goes a long way.
Chain order matters: render scene → bloom → color grade → vignette/grain → output. Each pass is a fullscreen quad — profile the chain; passes add up.

example.code:
Minimal post chain (GLSL-ish):
  vec3 c = texture(scene, uv).rgb;
  c += bloom(uv) * 0.6;              // glow
  c = grade(c);                      // lift/gamma/gain
  c *= 1.0 - 0.4 * length(uv - 0.5); // vignette
  c += (hash(uv + time) - 0.5) * 0.05; // grain
  gl_FragColor = vec4(c, 1.0);
example.walkthrough: Post-processing is where 'rendered' becomes 'cinematic'. Learn the chain order and the big four (bloom, grade, vignette, grain) — they cover 90% of looks.

pitfalls: Too much of everything — restraint is the skill; each effect at 60% of your first instinct.
Wrong chain order — grain before bloom looks wrong; learn the canonical order.
No performance budget — 6 fullscreen passes at 4K is heavy; profile on target hardware.
lessons.try_it: Add vignette + grain to any shader you have. A/B the result — feel the production value.

lessons.title: Live Performance Setup
concepts: The rig: laptop (performance machine, not dev machine) + audio interface + MIDI controller + projector/output. Redundancy for the critical path: backup laptop with the same set.
Rehearse the failure: what happens if the audio drops? If the projector disconnects? Have a fallback visual (a beautiful idle loop) that runs with zero input.
MIDI mapping: knobs for the 4-6 parameters you will actually touch live. Label them. Practice the set twice — muscle memory, not menu diving.
Audio routing: separate the performance audio from system sounds (do not let a notification ding through the PA). Dedicated interface, muted system.
Record every set (screen + room): the documentation IS the portfolio. A great set nobody recorded is a rumor.

example.code:
Pre-show checklist:
  [ ] Backup laptop synced + tested
  [ ] Idle-loop fallback verified (kill audio → still beautiful)
  [ ] MIDI mapped + labeled, 2 rehearsals done
  [ ] System sounds muted, notifications off
  [ ] Recording armed (screen + room camera)
  [ ] Power: laptop plugged, UPS if the venue is sketchy
example.walkthrough: Live performance is 20% visuals, 80% reliability. The audience remembers the crash, not the peak — engineer for no crashes.

pitfalls: No backup machine — one kernel panic ends the show.
No fallback visual — dead input = dead screen; idle loops save shows.
Unrehearsed MIDI — menu-diving on stage reads as amateur; practice the physical set.
lessons.try_it: Write the pre-show checklist for a hypothetical 20-minute set. What is your fallback visual?

lessons.title: Budgeting an Installation
concepts: Budget categories: hardware (projectors, PCs, sensors), fabrication (mounts, enclosures), venue (power, rigging, insurance), labor (install, tech), contingency (20% minimum).
The 2x rule: installations cost 2x the hardware in labor/logistics. A $5k projector is a $10k line item installed. Budget honestly or bleed later.
Contingency is not optional: 20% for known-unknowns (mount doesn't fit, cable too short), more for outdoor/temporary venues. Spend it or return it — but budget it.
Maintenance budget: who fixes it in month 3? Include a service retainer or train venue staff with the handover doc. Unmaintained installations die publicly.
Get 3 quotes for big items; buy once for critical path (projector, PC). Cheap critical hardware fails at the worst moment — the opening.

example.code:
Sample $25k budget:
  Hardware: $9k (projector, PC, sensors, cables)
  Fabrication: $3k (mounts, enclosure)
  Venue/logistics: $4k (power, rigging, insurance)
  Labor: $5k (install 3 days + tech)
  Contingency (20%): $4k
  Total: $25k. Every line justified; nothing hidden.
example.walkthrough: Budgeting is design: the numbers force decisions about scope before the venue does. Write the budget before the proposal — it keeps promises honest.

pitfalls: No contingency — the first surprise comes from your fee.
Hardware-only budgeting — labor and logistics are half the cost; budget them.
No maintenance plan — the piece dies slowly in public; budget the afterlife.
lessons.try_it: Budget a hypothetical small installation (one projector, one PC). Use the categories above. What is the total?

lessons.title: Composition Rules That Work
concepts: Rule of thirds: place focal points at the 1/3 intersections — not centered. Centered compositions feel static; offset feels dynamic.
Visual hierarchy: one dominant element, supporting elements, background. If everything shouts, nothing is heard — establish the pecking order.
Negative space is a material: the empty areas shape the full ones. Crowded canvases exhaust; breathing room focuses attention.
Color temperature guides the eye: warm advances, cool recedes. Use temperature to build depth without perspective.

example.code:
Sketch the same scene twice: once centered, once on thirds.
Compare: the thirds version almost always feels more 'designed'.
The rule is a starting point, not a prison —
break it deliberately once you feel it.
example.walkthrough: Composition is the silent half of every artwork: learn the rules so your breaks read as choices, not accidents.

pitfalls: Centering everything — the default that reads as amateur; offset deliberately.
Equal visual weight everywhere — no hierarchy means no focus; pick a hero.
Ignoring negative space — emptiness is compositional material, not waste.
lessons.try_it: Take any sketch. Apply rule of thirds + one dominant element. Compare before/after.

lessons.title: Drawing with Code: Curves and Paths
concepts: Bezier curves: two endpoints + control points. The control points are magnets — the curve bends toward them without touching (usually).
Quadratic vs cubic: quadratic has 1 control point (simple arcs); cubic has 2 (S-curves). Cubic covers nearly everything; quadratic is cheaper.
Polyline smoothing: Chaikin's corner-cutting turns jagged lines into smooth curves iteratively. Two iterations transform the feel.
Stroke as shape: varying width along a path (tapered strokes) adds calligraphic life. Simulate with offset curves or segment circles.

example.code:
Chaikin smoothing (pseudocode):
  for each corner P[i],P[i+1]:
    Q = 0.75*P[i] + 0.25*P[i+1]
    R = 0.25*P[i] + 0.75*P[i+1]
  Replace polyline with Q,R sequence. Repeat 2x.
  Jagged → flowing. The algorithm is 5 lines.
example.walkthrough: Curves are the vocabulary of organic form in code: master beziers and smoothing and your line work transforms.

pitfalls: Straight segments everywhere — code defaults to angular; curves need intention.
Too many control points — fewer, well-placed points make cleaner curves.
Ignoring stroke variation — uniform width reads as mechanical; taper for life.
lessons.try_it: Draw a flowing line using Chaikin smoothing on a jagged input. Two iterations; observe the change.

lessons.title: Particle Systems from Scratch
concepts: Anatomy: emitter (birth rate, position, spread) → particles (pos, vel, life, size, color) → updater (physics per frame) → renderer (draw alive). Four parts, endless variety.
Life as normalized age: age/lifespan drives size, alpha, color over time. The life curve IS the aesthetic — design it deliberately.
Forces: gravity, drag, turbulence (noise-based), attraction. Compose 2-3 forces; more becomes mush. Constraint breeds character.
Pooling: recycle dead particles instead of allocating. At 10k particles, allocation churn kills the frame rate — pool everything.

example.code:
Fire particle:
  emitter: 60/sec, upward cone spread
  vel: up 2 + noise; life: 1.5s
  color: yellow→orange→red→transparent (by life)
  size: grows then fades; gravity: slight up (hot air)
  forces: turbulence 0.3. Pool size: 200.
  Tune the life curve — it makes the fire.
example.walkthrough: Particles are the atoms of motion graphics: learn the four-part anatomy once, then it's all tuning life curves and forces.

pitfalls: Allocating per particle — pool; GC pauses murder frame rates.
Linear life curves — real phenomena ease; design the curve.
Too many forces — 2-3 composed forces; more is visual noise.
lessons.try_it: Build the fire particle above. Then make smoke by changing 4 parameters. Note how little changes.

lessons.title: Timeline Choreography
concepts: Choreography = timing relationships: sequence (A then B), overlap (B starts at 70% of A), stagger (each +100ms). The relationships carry the meaning.
Easing per relationship: entrances ease-out, exits ease-in, emphases use overshoot. Match the easing to the narrative beat.
The 12 principles (condensed): squash/stretch, anticipation, staging, follow-through, timing. Five of the twelve cover 90% of UI/game motion.
Scrub-ability: drive animation by a single t parameter so it can be scrubbed, reversed, paused. Time as input, not as side effect — testable and controllable.

example.code:
Button press choreography:
  t=0.0: anticipation (scale 0.95, 80ms, ease-in)
  t=0.08: press (scale 0.9, 60ms)
  t=0.14: release overshoot (scale 1.05, 120ms, ease-out)
  t=0.26: settle (scale 1.0, 100ms)
  Total 360ms. Feels alive; linear would feel dead.
example.walkthrough: Choreography turns animation from 'things moving' into communication: every timing relationship tells the user something. Design the relationships.

pitfalls: Everything simultaneous — stagger creates hierarchy and readability.
Linear everything — easing is the difference between motion and life.
Unscrubbable time — parameterize by t; debugging animation needs a timeline.
lessons.try_it: Choreograph a 3-element entrance (stagger 100ms, ease-out). Scrub it. Feel the difference vs simultaneous.

lessons.title: L-Systems: Drawing with Grammars
concepts: L-systems: an alphabet, an axiom, production rules. Iterate the rules, then interpret the string as drawing commands (turtle graphics). Grammar becomes form.
Classic: Koch snowflake (F → F+F−−F+F), plant branching (X → F−[[X]+X]+F[+FX]−X). A few rules generate botanical complexity.
Parameters: angle, step shrink per iteration, iteration count (3-6 typical). Small changes → wildly different plants. The parameter space is the garden.
Stochastic L-systems: rules with probabilities (X → ... 70%, ... 30%). Deterministic grammar gives species; stochastic gives individuals.

example.code:
Algae (Lindenmayer's original):
  Alphabet: A, B. Axiom: A.
  Rules: A → AB, B → A.
  Iterations: A → AB → ABA → ABAAB → ...
  Lengths: 1,2,3,5,8 — Fibonacci emerges from grammar.
  Two rules; the golden ratio appears.
example.walkthrough: L-systems prove that complexity needs no complexity: tiny grammars iterated produce organic richness. Rules × iteration = nature.

pitfalls: Too many iterations — exponential growth; 6+ iterations explode string length.
Ignoring the interpretation — the turtle parameters (angle, shrink) matter as much as the grammar.
Pure determinism — stochastic rules add the individuality that reads as 'natural'.
lessons.try_it: Implement the algae L-system. Iterate 6 times; verify the Fibonacci lengths. Then add a plant rule.

lessons.title: Agent-Based Emergence
concepts: Agents: simple entities with local rules (separation, alignment, cohesion for flocks; wander + deposit for slime molds). Global patterns emerge — no conductor.
The substrate matters: agents depositing into a shared field (trails, pheromones) create stigmergic coordination — communication through the environment.
Parameters to tune: sensor angle/distance, turn rate, deposit amount, decay rate. The phase space between chaos and order is where the beauty lives.
Capture the trails: render the field (not the agents) with slow fade. The accumulated history IS the artwork — agents are just the brushes.

example.code:
Slime mold sketch:
  1000 agents; each: sense 3 points ahead (angle ±45°),
    turn toward strongest trail, move 1px, deposit 1.
  Field: decay 0.99/frame, diffuse slightly.
  Render field as brightness. Run 2000 frames.
  Veins and networks emerge. No vein was programmed.
example.walkthrough: Agent systems are emergence you can tune: the local rules are simple, the global beauty is not. Tune the phase space, capture the trails.

pitfalls: Rendering agents not trails — the field history is the art; agents are brushes.
No decay — trails saturate to white; decay creates the dynamics.
Too few agents — emergence needs population; 1000+ for molds, 100+ for flocks.
lessons.try_it: Build the slime mold (or flocking). Tune sensor angle until networks emerge. Screenshot the phase transition.

lessons.title: Pointer as Material
concepts: The pointer is continuous input: position, velocity, pressure (where available), hover vs touch. Design for the STREAM, not the click.
Velocity matters: fast gestures = energy (throw, fling); slow = precision (draw, aim). Map velocity to response — the same input means different things at different speeds.
Trails and echoes: render pointer history (fading trail, delayed followers). The history visualizes the gesture — interaction becomes visible.
Multi-pointer: track each touch independently. Pinch, multi-draw, collaborative canvases — the pointer was never singular on touch devices.

example.code:
Velocity brush:
  speed = dist(p, prev) / dt
  width = map(speed, 0, fast, thick, thin)  // fast = thin, energetic
  alpha = map(speed, slow, fast, 0.9, 0.3)
  Render segment with width + alpha.
  The gesture's energy becomes the line's character.
example.walkthrough: Treat the pointer as a material with properties (position, velocity, pressure) — not as a button-presser. The stream is the medium.

pitfalls: Click-only thinking — the stream between clicks is where expression lives.
Ignoring velocity — same path, different speeds, should feel different.
Single-pointer assumptions — touch devices are multi-pointer; design for it.
lessons.try_it: Build the velocity brush. Draw fast vs slow strokes; feel the mapping. Adjust until it feels right.

lessons.title: Sound as Input, Light as Output
concepts: The loop: microphone/analysis → features (amplitude, FFT bands, onset) → mapping → visuals. The mapping IS the instrument — design it musically.
Onset detection: sudden energy increases = beats/events. Trigger visual events on onsets; modulate continuous visuals with band energies. Rhythm drives, texture flows.
Latency budget: <50ms feels connected; >100ms feels broken. Optimize the analysis chain — small FFT windows, efficient mapping.
Fallback: no-audio mode with an internal beat generator. The piece must work in silent rooms — design the silence case first.

example.code:
Kick-reactive pulse:
  FFT band 40-120Hz energy → smoothed (attack fast, release slow)
  Onset (energy jump > threshold) → trigger ring burst
  Continuous: band energy → background pulse scale
  Smoothing: fast attack (10ms), slow release (300ms) —
    the release curve IS the feel.
example.walkthrough: Audio-reactive work is instrument design: the mapping from sound features to visuals is the composition. Tune the smoothing — it's the musicality.

pitfalls: No smoothing — raw FFT is jittery; attack/release curves make it musical.
Ignoring latency — the beat-to-visual delay must stay under 50ms.
No silent fallback — the piece dies without audio; design the silence case.
lessons.try_it: Build onset detection on any audio. Trigger one visual event per onset. Tune the threshold until it grooves.

lessons.title: Documentation That Sells
concepts: The 3 artifacts: hero video (30-60s, the hook), process shots (build photos, sketches — proof of craft), technical write-up (how it works — proof of depth). All three, every project.
Hero video rules: start with the best 3 seconds, no intro titles, show interaction (hands touching, people reacting). The viewer decides in 5 seconds.
Process > polish in the write-up: the failed approach, the constraint that shaped the design, the number that mattered. Struggle is credibility.
Captions carry the context: where, when, for whom, your role, the tech. A beautiful image without context is decoration; with context, it's a case study.

example.code:
Project page skeleton:
  1. Hero video (autoplay, muted, 45s)
  2. One-line: what it is + where it showed
  3. 3 process images with captions
  4. 'How it works' (150 words + diagram)
  5. 'What I'd change' (honesty = credibility)
  6. Tech list + your role + collaborators
example.walkthrough: Document as you build, not after: the process shots only exist if you capture them during. Documentation is a build-phase activity.

pitfalls: Only finished glamour shots — process proves craft; polish alone invites doubt.
No context — where/when/role/tech; without it, it's just pretty.
Skipping 'what I'd change' — the honest reflection is what clients remember.
lessons.try_it: Pick one project. Write the one-line + 'what I'd change' now. Capture 3 process shots of current work this week.

lessons.title: Applying to Festivals and Grants
concepts: The package: artist statement (who you are, 150 words), project proposal (what + why + how, 300 words), portfolio (5 best, not 20), budget (real numbers), timeline. Same package, adapted per call.
Read the call like a brief: theme, venue constraints, tech provided, selection criteria. Proposals that answer the ACTUAL call win; generic ones don't.
Budget honesty: real quotes, 20% contingency, your labor costed. Funders smell fantasy budgets; honest ones with contingency signal professionalism.
Rejection is data: ask for feedback, track which proposals advance, iterate the package. The 10th application converts better than the 1st — if you learn.

example.code:
Proposal paragraph:
  'Lumen Drift is a 12-projector facade piece for [venue's] brick
   texture — the mapping exploits the mortar lines as rhythm.
   3 nights, dusk-midnight, silent (respecting residents).
   Budget $18k: $7k gear rental, $5k labor, $3k venue, $3k contingency.'
  Specific to the venue. That's the whole game.
example.walkthrough: Festival applications are design problems: the constraint (theme, venue, budget) shapes the proposal. Answer the call that's actually written.

pitfalls: Generic proposals — venue-blind applications lose to specific ones.
Fantasy budgets — no contingency, free labor; funders see through it.
Portfolio dumps — 5 best, curated to the call; 20 random works dilute.
lessons.try_it: Find one open call. Write the 300-word proposal paragraph for a hypothetical piece. Specific to their venue.

lessons.title: Teaching and Workshops as Income
concepts: Workshops are products: title, outcomes ('build X in 3 hours'), level, materials list, price. Productize the teaching — vague workshops don't sell.
The 3-hour format: 30min concepts, 90min guided build, 45min free experiment, 15min show-and-tell. The show-and-tell IS the marketing — participants share it.
Price on value + prep: a 3-hour workshop needs 10+ hours of prep initially. Price covers prep + delivery + materials; raise as the material matures.
Venues: festivals (paid slots), universities (guest lectures → courses), companies (creative team offsites pay best), online (scale, lower price). Diversify the channels.

example.code:
Workshop one-sheet:
  'Shaders in 3 Hours: from first triangle to post-processing'
  Level: creative coders with JS basics
  Take-home: 5 working sketches + cheat sheet
  Materials: laptop + browser (nothing to install)
  Price: $85/person, 20 max. Next: [date].
example.walkthrough: Teaching compounds: every workshop improves the material, grows the audience, and pays. The 10th delivery is 3x better than the 1st — start now.

pitfalls: Vague descriptions — 'intro to creative coding' doesn't sell; outcomes do.
Underpricing prep — 10+ hours of prep is real; price it in.
No take-home — participants need the artifact; it's the retention and the referral.
lessons.try_it: Outline a 3-hour workshop you could teach. Title, outcomes, the 4 time blocks. That's the product.

lessons.title: Composition Grids for Generative Layouts
concepts: A composition grid divides the canvas into a modular structure (columns, rows, margins) that gives generative elements a shared alignment system — randomness placed on a grid reads as intentional, while ungridded randomness reads as noise.

The rule of thirds, golden-ratio divisions, and 12-column grids are starting points, not laws: the grid's job is to create relationships between elements (alignment, rhythm, hierarchy), so choose divisions that serve the piece's focal logic.

Break the grid deliberately: place 80% of elements on-grid for coherence and let 20% break it for tension. A broken grid only reads as intentional when the grid itself is visible in the rest of the composition.
Responsive grids recompute from canvas dimensions (margins as fractions, gutters proportional) so the composition survives resize — hardcoded pixel grids shatter on different screens.

example.walkthrough: Compute the grid from live canvas dimensions so it survives resize. Place most elements at grid-derived positions for alignment, then let a controlled fraction break the grid for tension. The viewer perceives the system even where it's violated — that's what makes the break meaningful.

pitfalls: Hardcoding pixel grid values that break on any canvas size other than the one you designed on.
Placing EVERYTHING on-grid, producing sterile, spreadsheet-like compositions with no focal energy.
Using a grid but hiding it completely — if no alignment is visible, the grid added work without adding coherence.
lessons.try_it: Build a 12-column generative poster: 30 elements, 80% grid-aligned, 20% breaking the grid — then resize the canvas and verify the composition holds.

lessons.title: Easing Curves: From Linear to Spring
concepts: Easing maps linear progress (0→1) to eased progress: ease-out (fast start, gentle landing) suits entrances; ease-in (slow start, fast end) suits exits; ease-in-out suits transitions between visible states.
Cubic-bezier curves are the lingua franca — CSS, canvas, and animation libraries all speak them — so learning to read and author bezier handles transfers across every tool you'll use.
Overshoot easings (back, elastic) add physical character but must be used sparingly: one overshooting element is delightful; ten is seasickness. Reserve them for the primary focal action.

Spring physics (stiffness, damping, mass) beats fixed easings when targets move: a spring re-solves every frame, so interrupted or chained animations stay physical where bezier tweens would snap or restart.

example.walkthrough: For fixed A→B tweens, pick the easing that matches the narrative (entrances ease-out, exits ease-in). When the target can change mid-flight — dragging, live data, interaction — switch to the spring: it has no duration to restart, it just re-solves toward the new target every frame.

pitfalls: Using ease-in-out for everything — it makes entrances feel sluggish and exits feel floaty.
Stacking overshoot easings on multiple elements, creating visual chaos instead of character.
Restarting fixed-duration tweens on rapidly changing targets instead of switching to spring physics.
lessons.try_it: Animate a card entrance with ease-out, its exit with ease-in, then convert a draggable element from tween to spring and compare the feel when you change direction mid-drag.

lessons.title: Seeded Randomness and Edition Control
concepts: Math.random() is unseedable by design — every run is a new universe you can never revisit. A seeded PRNG (mulberry32, sfc32) turns 'random' into a deterministic function of the seed: same seed + same code = same artwork, forever.
Seeds are the edition mechanism for generative art: the collector owns seed #4821, you can re-render it at any resolution, and the provenance is verifiable (re-run the seed, compare the output).

Seed hygiene matters: use one PRNG stream per concern (layout stream, color stream, detail stream) so tweaking colors doesn't reshuffle the layout — or use a single stream but document that ANY code change re-rolls everything downstream.
Curate by exploration: generate 100 seeds, pick 5, refine the system, repeat. The seed browser (grid of thumbnails per seed) is the generative artist's contact sheet.

example.walkthrough: Replace every Math.random() call with your seeded rand(). Record the seed alongside each rendered variant — in the filename, the metadata, the edition certificate. When a collector asks for 'that one from the show,' you re-run the seed instead of mourning the lost frame.

pitfalls: Mixing Math.random() into a seeded system 'just for this one thing' — it poisons reproducibility silently.
Changing code after promising a collector their seed — the same seed now renders something different.
Using one global stream so that adding a single random call reshuffles the entire composition downstream.
lessons.try_it: Convert a sketch to mulberry32, render seeds 1–9 as thumbnails, pick your favorite, and prove reproducibility by re-rendering it after a restart.

lessons.title: Designing Affordances for Public Interaction
concepts: An affordance is a visual hint that says 'you can touch this': pulsing outlines, hover ripples, elements that lean toward the cursor. In public space, affordances replace instruction manuals — nobody reads the plaque.

The 3-second rule: a first-time visitor must discover the interaction and get rewarded within 3 seconds of noticing the piece. Design the attract state specifically to teach the gesture, not just to look pretty idle.

Feedback must be immediate (<100ms) and proportional: the visuals should respond to the FIRST pixel of movement, and bigger gestures should produce bigger responses. Laggy or binary feedback kills exploration.

Design for the full ability range: interaction that requires precise pointing excludes kids, elders, and wheelchair users. Favor gross-motor gestures (presence, large waves, body position) over fine-motor ones.

example.walkthrough: Build the attract state as a teacher: let it visibly track presence so visitors learn 'it sees me' before they gesture. When the first real gesture arrives, over-reward it — the outsized response teaches 'my actions matter here' and converts a tentative wave into play.

pitfalls: Hiding the interaction behind a 'touch to begin' button that nobody touches because they don't know it's interactive.
Rewarding only large, fast gestures — the hesitant first wave gets nothing and the visitor walks away.
Designing for your own dexterity instead of a tired 8-year-old or a 70-year-old with a cane.
lessons.try_it: Watch three strangers approach an interactive piece (yours or anyone's): note the exact second each discovers the interaction, and what taught them. Redesign one affordance based on what you saw.

lessons.title: Trigonometry for Organic Motion
concepts: Sine and cosine are the atoms of organic motion: x = cx + cos(a)*r gives circular orbits, and layering sines of different frequencies (a Lissajous approach) produces the complex-but-smooth paths that read as 'alive' rather than mechanical.
Phase offsets are the secret ingredient: ten particles with the same sine but staggered phases read as a wave or a school of fish; identical phases read as a rigid marching band.
Map angle to time, not frames: angle = t * speed keeps motion frame-rate independent and deterministic, while angle += per-frame accumulates drift and speed differences across displays.
Combine trig with easing on the amplitude: a sine whose radius breathes (r = base + sin(t*0.3)*amp) gives the 'breathing' quality that separates organic motion from clockwork.

example.walkthrough: Start with a plain circular orbit, then add a second sine at a non-integer frequency ratio for Lissajous drift. Stagger the phase per particle to get schooling behavior. Finally, modulate the radius with a slow sine — that breathing amplitude is what the eye reads as organic.

pitfalls: Incrementing angle per frame instead of deriving it from elapsed time, causing speed to vary with frame rate.
Using integer frequency ratios only, which produce closed, repetitive, visibly mechanical loops.
Giving every particle the same phase — synchronized motion reads as robotic, not organic.
lessons.try_it: Build 50 orbiting particles with staggered phases and breathing radii; then change one frequency ratio from 1.0 to 1.618 and observe the motion become non-repeating.

lessons.title: Noise Fields: Beyond Random
concepts: White noise (Math.random()) has no memory — each value is independent, which is why it looks harsh and jittery. Perlin/simplex noise is coherent: nearby inputs give nearby outputs, producing the smooth natural variation of clouds, terrain, and flow fields.

A flow field samples noise per particle per frame: angle = noise(x*s, y*s, t*s) * TAU. Particles follow the field's direction, and the field evolves over time — this single technique generates smoke, crowds, hair, and water.

Octaves stack detail: base noise gives the large shapes, each added octave (double frequency, half amplitude) adds finer detail. 3–4 octaves is the sweet spot; more octaves cost performance for detail nobody sees.
Domain-warping (sampling noise at noise-distorted coordinates) turns bland fields into marbled, turbulent, organic structures — it's the difference between a smooth gradient and marble.

example.walkthrough: Sample 2D noise at each particle's position (scaled small so the field varies smoothly across the canvas) plus a time component so the field evolves. Steer particles along the field angle. Then warp: offset the sample coordinates by another noise value to get turbulent, marbled flow instead of smooth laminar flow.

pitfalls: Sampling noise at too large a scale (looks random) or too small (looks flat) — scale is the whole game.
Forgetting the time dimension, producing a beautiful but frozen field.
Stacking 8 octaves 'for quality' and melting the frame rate for invisible detail.
lessons.try_it: Build a 2,000-particle flow field; then add domain warping and compare screenshots — note how the same particle count produces radically richer structure.

lessons.title: L-Systems and Fractal Growth
concepts: An L-system is a rewriting grammar: an axiom (starting string) plus production rules (each symbol rewrites to a string). Iterating the rewrite N times grows complex branching structures from tiny rules — the classic model of plant growth.
Turtle graphics interprets the string: F = draw forward, + / - = turn, [ = push state, ] = pop state. The bracket stack is what creates branches — without it you get a line, with it you get a tree.

Stochastic L-systems (rules chosen probabilistically per rewrite) grow every plant differently from the same grammar — combine with seeded randomness and you get a reproducible forest, not a cloned tree.
Iteration depth is exponential: each level multiplies string length by the rule's expansion factor. Depth 6–8 is plenty; beyond that you're drawing millions of segments for sub-pixel detail.

example.walkthrough: Start with axiom F and one rule. Iterate the rewrite 5 times and watch the string explode in length — that's the growth. Interpret it with a turtle where brackets push/pop position and heading, giving you branches. Then make the turn angle and rule choice stochastic (seeded) for a natural, non-cloned tree.

pitfalls: Iterating too deep — the string grows exponentially and the draw call count explodes past what's visible.
Forgetting the bracket stack, producing a single wandering line instead of branching structure.
Using identical angles everywhere, which reads as fractal-mathematical rather than botanical — nature jitters.
lessons.try_it: Grow a stochastic L-system tree at depth 5 with seeded jitter on angles; render 4 variants and pick the most tree-like — then explain what made it win.

lessons.title: Curating a Coherent Showcase Page
concepts: A showcase page argues a thesis about your practice, not an inventory of your output. Every piece either advances the argument or dilutes it — the cuts are the curation.

Order for the skim reader: lead with the strongest, most representative piece (the 3-second test), then sequence by narrative (evolution, scale, or theme) — never chronological by default, which buries the best work under old work.

Each piece needs the same four beats: the hook visual, what it is (one line), what it does (interaction/system, one line), and the proof (video or live embed). Missing beats make curators bounce to the next tab.
Performance is curation too: lazy-load live pieces, poster-frame everything below the fold, and cap total page weight. A showcase that stutters tells the curator your work stutters.

example.walkthrough: Structure each entry identically: poster image for instant load, a one-line what-it-is, a one-line what-it-does, and a 60-second video. Offer live versions behind an explicit play button — the visitor opts into the performance cost, and your page stays fast for the skim reader deciding in 10 seconds.

pitfalls: Auto-running five WebGL pieces on page load, melting the visitor's laptop before they've seen anything.
Leading with your oldest work chronologically, so the first impression is your weakest.
Inconsistent documentation depth — three videos on one piece, a single blurry still on the next — which reads as uneven practice.
lessons.try_it: Audit your showcase page with a 10-second skim test: show it to someone for 10 seconds, then ask what your work is about. Cut or reorder until their answer matches your thesis.

lessons.title: Writing Festival Applications That Get Read
concepts: Juries skim: your application gets 2–3 minutes. The first paragraph must carry the whole proposal — what it is, what the visitor experiences in 30 seconds, and why this festival. Everything after is evidence.

Fit beats prestige: juries select work that serves THEIR audience and space. A proposal that names the festival's context (outdoor night program, family audience, specific venue) outscores a generic masterpiece statement every time.

The 60-second video is the application: juries watch it before reading. It must show the interaction loop (input → response) and audience reaction — stills and artist statements don't survive the skim.
Technical feasibility is scored: include a one-page rider (power, space, setup time, crew needs) that proves you've thought about their venue. 'We'll figure it out' reads as risk.

example.code:
Paragraph 1: 'Lumen Field is a 20m interactive light floor where visitors\' footsteps bloom into slow-fading color fields. In your night program, 200 visitors/hour would play across it; setup is 6 hours with 2 crew, 2x 16A circuits.'
Para 2-3: the work's context and your track record. Rider: one page.
example.walkthrough: Write paragraph one as if it's the only thing read — because it might be. Name their festival, their audience, their constraints. Attach the 60-second interaction video and the one-page rider. Then stop: brevity signals professionalism to an overloaded jury.

pitfalls: Submitting the same generic statement to every festival — juries smell it instantly.
Proposing unbuilt large-scale work you can't deliver if selected — a reputation-ending move.
Burying the visitor experience under technical description; juries program experiences, not architectures.

lessons.title: Grant Narratives for Media Art
concepts: Panels fund missions, not technologies: translate your technical approach into the visitor's experience and the funder's stated priorities. Mirror their language — if they fund 'community engagement,' your piece creates 'shared moments of play for intergenerational audiences.'
The budget is a narrative document: every line should map to the project description. Reviewers cross-check — a $3,000 'materials' line with no materials mentioned in the narrative reads as padding.
Public benefit must be specific and measurable: 'free outdoor performances for an estimated 5,000 visitors over 3 weekends, with documented workshops for 60 youth' beats 'enriches the community.'
Feasibility proof lives in the timeline and work samples, not adjectives: a week-by-week plan with milestones and 2–3 relevant past works proves you can deliver what the narrative promises.

example.walkthrough: Open with the visitor's experience, not your system. Translate the tech into one plain sentence that proves feasibility without jargon. Tie every budget line to a narrative element. Close with the measurable public benefit — numbers of people, sessions, access — that the panel can defend to their board.

pitfalls: Writing for engineers when the panel is artists, curators, and community members.
Vague public benefit ('enriches culture') that no panelist can quote when advocating for your proposal.
A budget that doesn't match the narrative — the fastest way to lose a reviewer's trust.
lessons.try_it: Take your project description and rewrite the opening paragraph for a non-technical panelist; then check every budget line against the narrative and flag orphans.

lessons.title: Your First Fragment Shader
concepts: A fragment shader is a program that runs once per pixel: it receives interpolated values (like UV coordinates) and outputs a color. All the 'magic' is math on uv — there are no shapes, no draw calls, just a function from coordinate to color.

uv coordinates (0→1 across the screen) are your canvas: smoothstep(uv.x) is a gradient, length(uv-0.5) is a radial distance, fract(uv*10.) is a grid. Every classic shader effect is a composition of these primitives.
Uniforms are the shader's inputs from your code: u_time for animation, u_resolution for aspect correction, u_mouse for interaction. The shader itself is stateless — all change comes through uniforms.
Aspect correction is the first bug everyone hits: without dividing uv.x by (width/height), circles render as ellipses on widescreen. Fix it once, in every shader, forever.

example.walkthrough: Normalize pixel coordinates to uv, fix the aspect ratio, then compute a radial distance from center. Modulate a color mix by that distance and a time-based pulse traveling outward. Every line is a reusable primitive — distance fields, smoothstep falloffs, time modulation — that composes into all future shaders.

pitfalls: Forgetting aspect correction — every circle becomes an ellipse and you blame the math.
Treating the shader as stateful: trying to 'remember' previous frames without a feedback texture.
Debugging by staring: output intermediate values as colors (the shader debugger) instead of guessing.
lessons.try_it: Write the pulsing radial shader above, then change the distance metric to length(uv-vec2) with different centers per color channel for chromatic aberration.

lessons.title: Post-Processing Chains
concepts: A post-processing chain renders the scene to a texture, then runs fullscreen passes over it: each pass reads the previous pass's output. The chain is a pipeline — order carries meaning, not just aesthetics.

Bloom first (it thresholds bright pixels — grain added before bloom gets amplified into sparkle), vignette second (darkens edges), grain LAST (it's a property of the final image; anything after it smears it).
Ping-pong framebuffers let passes feed back into themselves: two textures alternate as read/write targets, enabling feedback trails, fluid simulation, and iterative blur without allocating per frame.

Resolution is a creative control: compute expensive passes (blur, noise) at half or quarter resolution and upscale — the eye can't see the difference in smooth effects, but the GPU feels 4–16x less work.

example.walkthrough: Render your scene to a texture. Run bloom on it (bright-pass + blur), then vignette, then grain as the final pass. For feedback trails, ping-pong two textures: each frame reads the previous frame decayed by 0.96 and takes the max with the new render — motion leaves fading trails with zero CPU cost.

pitfalls: Putting grain before bloom and wondering why the image sparkles.
Allocating a new framebuffer per frame instead of ping-ponging two — a memory leak wearing a pipeline costume.
Running blur/noise at full 4K when quarter-resolution is visually identical and 16x cheaper.
lessons.try_it: Build a 3-pass chain (bloom → vignette → grain) on any scene; then swap the order to grain-first and screenshot the difference as proof of why order matters.

lessons.title: Mapping Audio Features to Visuals
concepts: Raw amplitude is the least musical signal: it has 60dB of dynamic range and says 'nothing' during quiet breakdowns. Musical features — bass energy, spectral centroid (brightness), onset detection (transients), beat phase — map to musical structure, not just loudness.

Split the spectrum into bands (bass/mids/highs) with per-band normalization: each band gets its own full visual range, so a quiet hi-hat pattern drives visuals as richly as the kick. Without per-band normalization, the loudest band owns the whole piece.

Attack/release smoothing mimics perception: fast attack (respond to onsets instantly) with slow release (decay gracefully) makes visuals feel glued to the music instead of flickering with every FFT frame.

Map features to visual dimensions with semantic fit: bass energy → scale/pulse (weight), spectral centroid → hue (brightness), beat phase → motion timing (groove). Arbitrary mappings feel random; semantic ones feel inevitable.

example.walkthrough: Pull frequency data per frame, average into bass/mid/high bands, and normalize each band against its own running peak. Smooth with asymmetric attack/release so onsets snap and decays glide. Map the features semantically — bass to pulse, brightness to hue — and the visuals will feel composed with the music rather than merely loud with it.

pitfalls: Mapping raw amplitude to size — dead during breakdowns, violent on drops.
One global normalization across the full spectrum, letting the kick drum starve every other band.
Symmetric smoothing that either flickers (too fast) or lags (too slow) — attack and release need different rates.
lessons.try_it: Build a 3-band visualizer with per-band normalization and attack/release; A/B it against a raw-amplitude version on the same track and note where each breaks.

lessons.title: Live Performance Fallback Design
concepts: Every live audio input WILL fail eventually: cables, mixer feeds, OS permission dialogs, browser autoplay policies. Design the fallback FIRST, not after the first dead show — the fallback is part of the piece, not an apology.

The trigger: when input energy stays below a calibrated threshold for N seconds (distinguishing silence-in-music from signal-loss via the threshold + duration), crossfade to autonomous mode. The crossfade (2–3 seconds) hides the transition; a hard cut announces the failure.

Autonomous mode should be seeded and tempo-aware: estimate BPM from pre-failure history and keep pulsing at that tempo, so the room feels continuity, not a screensaver. When signal returns, crossfade back.
Rehearse the failure: pull the cable in rehearsal and watch the transition. If you flinch, the audience will too. The fallback must be boring to you and invisible to them.

example.walkthrough: Run a watchdog on input energy with a 3-second persistence — brief musical silences won't trigger it, dead cables will. On trigger, crossfade over 2.5 seconds to a seeded generative mode pulsing at the BPM estimated from before the failure. Rehearse by yanking the cable: the transition should feel like a musical change, not a technical one.

pitfalls: Triggering fallback on every quiet breakdown — threshold without duration persistence.
Hard-cutting to fallback, which reads as 'something broke' to the whole room.
Autonomous mode at a random tempo that clashes with the DJ's actual set when signal returns.
Never rehearsing the failure — discovering your fallback is broken mid-show.
lessons.try_it: Implement the watchdog + crossfade on your audio piece; then pull the input in rehearsal and time how long before a viewer would notice. Tune until they wouldn't.

lessons.title: Hardware Selection for Installations
concepts: Select hardware by operational constraints, not specs: unattended runtime, dust/heat, theft risk, boot behavior, and remote recovery matter more than GPU benchmarks for a 3-month gallery run.

Fanless single-board computers win on reliability (no moving parts, no OS update surprises, boot straight into the piece) when the simplified version preserves the artistic intent. Full PCs win only when full fidelity IS the work.

Every component needs a spares plan: the sensor that dies in week 3, the cable that gets kicked, the SD card that corrupts. Spares on-site turn a crisis into a 10-minute swap; spares 'ordered when needed' turn it into a week dark.
Price the total operational cost, not the purchase price: PC ($1,800) + UPS + remote management + maintenance visits vs board ($150) + spares kit. The sticker price is the smallest line item.

example.code:
Decision matrix:
  Unattended 3 months, no IT staff, 1080p projection:
  -> fanless board + hardware watchdog (auto-reboot on hang)
     + on-site spares kit (board, PSU, cables, sensor)
     + remote heartbeat (screenshot ping every 5 min)
  Full 4K particle sim, artist on call:
  -> PC + UPS + remote desktop + maintenance contract
example.walkthrough: List the operational constraints first (duration, staffing, environment, fidelity needs), then score options against them. Default to the simplest hardware that preserves the art; add a hardware watchdog for auto-recovery and a heartbeat so you know it's alive without driving there. The spares kit is part of the hardware decision, not an afterthought.

pitfalls: Spec-sheet shopping: buying GPU power for a piece bottlenecked by sensor latency.
No watchdog timer — a hung piece stays hung until someone visits.
Forgetting theft/vandalism: a $1,800 PC in a public space needs a lock plan, not just a power plan.
lessons.try_it: Write the operational-constraints list for a hypothetical 2-month installation, then score a PC vs a single-board computer against it and justify the winner in three sentences.

lessons.title: Power and Safety Fundamentals
concepts: Do the load math: watts = volts × amps, and size supplies AND wiring for 125% of continuous load (electrical code for sustained draws). A 40A 12V LED run is 480W — size the supply for 600W and the wire gauge for 50A.
Warm cables are the warning: undersized conductors or daisy-chained extensions create resistance heat at every joint. Dedicated circuits beat extension chains; every joint is a future failure point.

Outdoor + public + electricity demands GFCI/RCD protection, weatherproof connections, and trip-proof cable runs (ramps, not tape). The safety plan is a legal document — it proves due diligence if anything goes wrong.
Anything above low-voltage gets a licensed electrician. Your art budget must include their hours; 'I'll wire the 240V myself' is how installations make the news.

example.code:
Load calc: 40A @ 12V = 480W continuous
  -> supply: 600W (125% rule)
  -> wire: 8 AWG for the 50A-rated run (not the 14 AWG extension cord)
  -> circuits: dedicated 20A mains circuit for supply + projector + PC
  -> protection: GFCI breaker (outdoor), cable ramps at crossings
example.walkthrough: Add up every load in watts, apply the 125% continuous-load rule to size the supply, then size the wire gauge for the resulting current — never the reverse. Run dedicated circuits instead of daisy chains, protect outdoor runs with GFCI, and ramp every public cable crossing. Document it all: the venue's safety sign-off depends on this sheet.

pitfalls: Daisy-chaining extension cords — each joint adds resistance and heat.
Sizing wire for the average load instead of the peak continuous load.
Skipping GFCI outdoors because 'it's only low voltage' — the MAINS side of your supply isn't.
No cable protection in public paths — a trip is a lawsuit, not an inconvenience.
lessons.try_it: Compute the full load sheet for an installation with LEDs, a projector, and a PC: watts per device, supply sizing at 125%, wire gauge, and circuit count. Get a venue tech to sanity-check it.

sections.heading: Interaction
items: Mouse input — implement touchStarted()/touchMoved() alongside (or instead of) mouse handlers, and return false to stop the browser scrolling/zooming over your canvas. mousePressed sometimes fires on mobile, but unreliably — dedicated touch handlers are the robust path.
Event functions — mousePressed() is an event: it fires once per click. mouseIsPressed is state: true for every frame the button stays down (dozens of frames per click).

Polling vs events — events for discrete actions (spawn, toggle), polling for continuous ones (dragging, holding). A mode variable with a switch in draw() — each case self-contained, transitions triggered by events or timers.
KeyPressed() with (key === ' ') toggles pause once per press — discrete.
